title: DRC: Religious Denominations Join Campaign for Genocide Recognition
excerpt: Kinshasa, DRC - On Friday, November 28, 2025, religious denominations across the Democratic Republic of Congo confirmed their support for the campaign promoting the recognition of the Congolese genocide, during a…
title_en: DRC: Religious Denominations Join Campaign for Genocide Recognition
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, DRC - On Friday, November 28, 2025, religious denominations across the Democratic Republic of Congo confirmed their support for the campaign promoting the recognition of the Congolese genocide, during a…
body_en:
Kinshasa, DRC - On Friday, November 28, 2025, religious denominations across the Democratic Republic of Congo confirmed their support for the campaign promoting the recognition of the Congolese genocide, during a meeting with Minister of Human Rights Samuel Mbemba in Kinshasa.

Pastors and imams from the platform pledged to disseminate the resolutions of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights and African civil society in their places of worship, reinforcing a shared understanding of the violence suffered in the eastern DRC.

Among the representatives, Archbishop Evariste Ejiba emphasized that this commitment would allow the Congolese people to speak with one voice. Minister Mbemba welcomed this support, noting that it strengthens an initiative led by President Félix Tshisekedi.

title: Walungu: 112 Civilians Killed in Eight Months Amid Clashes Between M23 and Wazalendo
excerpt: Walungu, November 22, 2025 - A coalition of human rights organizations in Walungu, South Kivu, released a deeply alarming report detailing at least 112 civilian deaths recorded between March and November 2025 during…
title_en: Walungu: 112 Civilians Killed in Eight Months Amid Clashes Between M23 and Wazalendo
excerpt_en: Walungu, November 22, 2025 - A coalition of human rights organizations in Walungu, South Kivu, released a deeply alarming report detailing at least 112 civilian deaths recorded between March and November 2025 during…
body_en:
Walungu, November 22, 2025 - A coalition of human rights organizations in Walungu, South Kivu, released a deeply alarming report detailing at least 112 civilian deaths recorded between March and November 2025 during clashes between the AFC/M23 rebels and the Wazalendo self-defense groups.

According to the report, the violence has ravaged the areas of Kaniola, Mulamba, Tubimbi, Kamisimbi, and Nyangezi, where civilians-including women and children-have been caught in a cycle of deadly confrontations. Investigators documented serious human rights violations, including rape, mass looting, and arbitrary arrests.

One of the most recent incidents highlighted is the November 20 arrest of two members of the same family in Kaniola, whose relatives say they remain without any information on their whereabouts. Rights defenders are calling for their immediate release and for urgent measures to protect civilians trapped in the conflict zones.

title: North Kivu: 29 Killed in ADF Attack on Byambwe
excerpt: Byambwe, Lubero Territory - November 17, 2025. The death toll from the deadly assault carried out by ADF rebels between Friday night, November 14, and Saturday morning, November 15, has risen to 29 victims, including 11…
title_en: North Kivu: 29 Killed in ADF Attack on Byambwe
excerpt_en: Byambwe, Lubero Territory - November 17, 2025. The death toll from the deadly assault carried out by ADF rebels between Friday night, November 14, and Saturday morning, November 15, has risen to 29 victims, including 11…
body_en:
Byambwe, Lubero Territory - November 17, 2025. The death toll from the deadly assault carried out by ADF rebels between Friday night, November 14, and Saturday morning, November 15, has risen to 29 victims, including 11 women and 7 men, according to local authorities. The attackers targeted the Byambwe health center and the surrounding village, inflicting severe civilian losses in a locality already hosting displaced families fleeing earlier violence.

In addition to the human toll, the assault caused extensive material damage, further aggravating the humanitarian situation in the area.

Colonel Alain Kiwewa, administrator of Lubero territory, condemned the attack as a crime against humanity, urging residents to reinforce support for the joint operations conducted by the FARDC and the Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF). These operations aim to pursue ADF fighters and restore security across the region, which has been plagued by recurrent insurgent attacks.

title: South Kivu: Bukavu-Miti-Hombo Road Blocked After Clashes Between M23 and Wazalendo
excerpt: Kabare Territory, November 17, 2025. Traffic on the Bukavu-Miti-Hombo road was completely paralyzed on Monday after violent clashes erupted between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters in South Kivu’s Kabare territory.
title_en: South Kivu: Bukavu-Miti-Hombo Road Blocked After Clashes Between M23 and Wazalendo
excerpt_en: Kabare Territory, November 17, 2025. Traffic on the Bukavu-Miti-Hombo road was completely paralyzed on Monday after violent clashes erupted between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters in South Kivu’s Kabare territory.
body_en:
Kabare Territory, November 17, 2025. Traffic on the Bukavu-Miti-Hombo road was completely paralyzed on Monday after violent clashes erupted between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters in South Kivu’s Kabare territory.

The confrontation, marked by the use of heavy and light weapons, forced motorcycle taxi drivers and other road users to turn back, severely disrupting local economic activity and isolating several communities.

According to local sources, the M23 was attempting to secure access routes toward villages under Wazalendo control, particularly Kalonge and Bunyakiri.

These incidents come shortly after FARDC spokesperson Major General Sylvain Ekenge issued a warning against any rebel advance. They also follow the recent fall of Maimingi 1 and 2, two villages in the Shabunda territory captured by the M23.

excerpt: Djugu Territory, November 18, 2025. The Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) have seized 108 AK-47 rifles, 4 PKM machine guns, and large quantities of ammunition and military equipment in multiple villages across Ituri’s…
title_en: Ituri: FARDC Discovers Major CRP Arms Caches, Seizing Over 100 Rifles
excerpt_en: Djugu Territory, November 18, 2025. The Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) have seized 108 AK-47 rifles, 4 PKM machine guns, and large quantities of ammunition and military equipment in multiple villages across Ituri’s…
body_en:
Djugu Territory, November 18, 2025. The Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) have seized 108 AK-47 rifles, 4 PKM machine guns, and large quantities of ammunition and military equipment in multiple villages across Ituri’s Djugu territory.

The operation targeted the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) militia led by Thomas Lubanga. According to military sources, the arms caches, abandoned and buried by retreating fighters, were uncovered in Mabanga, Nizi, Plito, Iga-Barrière, and areas near Lake Albert.

After six consecutive days of fighting and the destruction of several militia positions, local civil society welcomed the progress made by government forces. However, it also condemned recent abuses, notably illegal roadblocks erected by certain soldiers, which continue to increase the vulnerability of civilians already affected by insecurity.

title: North Kivu: Five Congolese Soldiers Repatriated After UPDF Intervention
excerpt: Kasindi-Lubiriha, November 17, 2025. Five Congolese soldiers who had fled the AFC/M23 occupation of Goma were officially handed over to the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) by the Ugandan army (UPDF) on Monday.
title_en: North Kivu: Five Congolese Soldiers Repatriated After UPDF Intervention
excerpt_en: Kasindi-Lubiriha, November 17, 2025. Five Congolese soldiers who had fled the AFC/M23 occupation of Goma were officially handed over to the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) by the Ugandan army (UPDF) on Monday.
body_en:
Kasindi-Lubiriha, November 17, 2025. Five Congolese soldiers who had fled the AFC/M23 occupation of Goma were officially handed over to the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) by the Ugandan army (UPDF) on Monday. The repatriation took place in Kasindi-Lubiriha, about 90 km from Beni.

The soldiers had been intercepted in July 2025 on Ugandan territory. According to the UPDF, they were protected under international humanitarian law, did not request asylum, and clearly expressed their intention to return to the DRC.

The handover ceremony, attended by authorities from both countries, was presided over by the military governor of North Kivu, General Évariste Somo Kakulé, who praised the strengthened bilateral cooperation at a time when the eastern region is facing persistent insecurity.

excerpt: Djugu, Ituri - November 17, 2025. More than 1,800 displaced people have returned to the villages of Limani, Iga-Barrière, Nizi, and Mangala in Djugu territory following a relative improvement in security, according to a…
title_en: Ituri: Over 1,800 Displaced People Return to Djugu Amid Fragile Calm
excerpt_en: Djugu, Ituri - November 17, 2025. More than 1,800 displaced people have returned to the villages of Limani, Iga-Barrière, Nizi, and Mangala in Djugu territory following a relative improvement in security, according to a…
body_en:
Djugu, Ituri - November 17, 2025. More than 1,800 displaced people have returned to the villages of Limani, Iga-Barrière, Nizi, and Mangala in Djugu territory following a relative improvement in security, according to a statement from the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).

This return has enabled the gradual reopening of schools and markets and aligns with the start of the agricultural season, allowing families to resume cultivation of their fields.

However, OCHA warns that the security situation remains fragile, noting ongoing food insecurity and the need for continued humanitarian assistance. The agency stresses that strengthened protection measures are essential to ensure the stability and resilience of these vulnerable communities.

title: North Kivu: Rising Tensions as AFC-M23 Expands Control in Masisi
excerpt: The security and humanitarian situation in Masisi territory (North Kivu) continues to deteriorate, with several localities falling under the control of AFC-M23 rebels after three days of intense clashes with the…
title_en: North Kivu: Rising Tensions as AFC-M23 Expands Control in Masisi
excerpt_en: The security and humanitarian situation in Masisi territory (North Kivu) continues to deteriorate, with several localities falling under the control of AFC-M23 rebels after three days of intense clashes with the…
body_en:
The security and humanitarian situation in Masisi territory (North Kivu) continues to deteriorate, with several localities falling under the control of AFC-M23 rebels after three days of intense clashes with the Congolese army and allied armed groups, from Sunday, November 17 to Wednesday, November 20.

This new wave of violence comes barely a week after the signing of a framework agreement in Doha, raising further doubts about its implementation on the ground. The rebel advance led to the capture of strategic villages including Kasheke, Bituna, the chief town of the Katoyi sector, as well as the chief town of the Nyamaboko 1 groupement.

Residents of Mweso and surrounding communities fled in large numbers, seeking safety as fighting approached their homes. Local authorities and civil society leaders report that the AFC-M23 has begun setting up a parallel administration in the newly seized areas, tightening its grip on the territory. Meanwhile, significant population movements toward neighboring Walikale are aggravating an already fragile humanitarian situation, with aid actors warning of escalating needs.

Masisi, North Kivu - After nearly a week of forced displacement following the occupation of Mahanga village (Nyamaboko 1 group, Masisi territory) by the AFC/M23 rebels, residents are gradually returning home. body_en:
Mwenga, South Kivu - Civil society groups are denouncing looting committed by soldiers, mainly deserters from the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) and fighters from the Wazalendo movement, in the towns of Kasika, Mwenga-Centre, and Kamituga.

Testimonies indicate that this looting is paralyzing daily life: businesses and schools are closed, and public transportation has halted. In Kamituga, gunfire erupted on November 25, 2025, when soldiers returning from the front attempted to loot. Burundian stabilization forces in the area reportedly intervened to prevent further violence.

Many residents have taken refuge in their homes for fear of attack, while civil society organizations are calling for urgent intervention to restore security and protect civilians.

title: North Kivu: UNICEF to Close Beni Office Amid Financial Constraints
excerpt: Beni, North Kivu, DRC - UNICEF confirmed on September 25, 2025, the upcoming closure of its Beni office due to financial constraints.
title_en: North Kivu: UNICEF to Close Beni Office Amid Financial Constraints
excerpt_en: Beni, North Kivu, DRC - UNICEF confirmed on September 25, 2025, the upcoming closure of its Beni office due to financial constraints.
body_en:
Beni, North Kivu, DRC - UNICEF confirmed on September 25, 2025, the upcoming closure of its Beni office due to financial constraints. The announcement was made by Foura Sassu Madi, head of the UNICEF office for North Kivu and Maniema, following discussions with the provincial vice-governor.

The restructuring comes amid a serious cash flow crisis, which has already led to the termination of contracts for nearly 130 employees in the DRC. UNICEF emphasized that this is not a full withdrawal: its Goma office will now coordinate all provincial activities. The organization assured that it will maintain sufficient operational and logistical capacity to continue its interventions throughout North Kivu.

Mwenga and Shabunda, South Kivu, DRC - Since Tuesday, November 25, 2025, violent clashes between AFC-M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC), supported by Wazalendo fighters, have rocked the Kirungutwe and Kasika areas of Mwenga territory. At least ten civilians have been killed, while thousands of residents have been forcibly displaced.

Accusations of looting have been leveled against both the FARDC and Wazalendo forces along the Kirungutwe-Kasika-Mwenga-Kamituga axis, paralyzing school and economic activities. Mutshatsha, Lualaba, DRC - A tragic landslide occurred at the Mulondo mining site in the Kawama district, claiming the lives of several young artisanal miners. title: DRC: ADF and M23 Identified as Deadliest Armed Groups in October - Kivu Security Barometer
excerpt: Kinshasa, DRC - According to the Kivu Security Barometer, published on November 24, 2025 by the Ebuteli Research Institute, the ADF and M23 were the deadliest armed groups in the Democratic Republic of Congo during October 2025.
title_en: DRC: ADF and M23 Identified as Deadliest Armed Groups in October - Kivu Security Barometer
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, DRC - According to the Kivu Security Barometer, published on November 24, 2025 by the Ebuteli Research Institute, the ADF and M23 were the deadliest armed groups in the Democratic Republic of Congo during October 2025.
body_en:
Kinshasa, DRC - According to the Kivu Security Barometer, published on November 24, 2025 by the Ebuteli Research Institute, the ADF and M23 were the deadliest armed groups in the Democratic Republic of Congo during October 2025. The report emphasizes the scale of violence in North Kivu, South Kivu, and Ituri provinces.

The ADF emerged as the most lethal group, particularly in terms of civilian casualties, despite receiving less media coverage than the M23. Henri Pacifique Mayala, an analyst at Ebuteli, notes that the widely publicized abuses of the M23 often overshadow the ADF's impact, whose attacks continue to inflict serious harm on the local population in eastern DRC.

This report underscores the persistent insecurity in the Great Lakes region, highlighting the urgent need for coordinated military, humanitarian, and governance responses to protect civilians and stabilize the affected areas.

title: DRC: European Union Grants €10 Million to FARDC to Strengthen Operational Capacities
excerpt: Kinshasa, DRC - The European Union announced on November 24, 2025, the provision of €10 million in additional funding to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC).
title_en: DRC: European Union Grants €10 Million to FARDC to Strengthen Operational Capacities
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, DRC - The European Union announced on November 24, 2025, the provision of €10 million in additional funding to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC).
body_en:
Kinshasa, DRC - The European Union announced on November 24, 2025, the provision of €10 million in additional funding to the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC). This funding is earmarked for the acquisition of non-lethal military equipment aimed at enhancing operational capacities, particularly in the areas of command and control, medical assistance, and surveillance patrols along river borders.

The first deliveries of this equipment are expected by the end of 2026. This contribution increases the total support provided by the European Peace Mechanism since 2023 to €30 million, complementing prior assistance to the 31st Rapid Reaction Brigade in Kindu.

The European Union emphasized that this funding is part of a broader effort to support security sector reform in the DRC, strengthen civilian protection missions, and restore state authority in conflict-affected zones, reinforcing the country's efforts to stabilize eastern DRC.

title: DRC: UN Reports Nearly 2,800 Human Rights Violations in First Half of 2025
excerpt: Kinshasa, DRC - The United Nations Joint Human Rights Office (UNJHRO) revealed in a press release on November 24, 2025, that it had recorded 2,767 human rights violations and breaches of international humanitarian law…
title_en: DRC: UN Reports Nearly 2,800 Human Rights Violations in First Half of 2025
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, DRC - The United Nations Joint Human Rights Office (UNJHRO) revealed in a press release on November 24, 2025, that it had recorded 2,767 human rights violations and breaches of international humanitarian law…
body_en:
Kinshasa, DRC - The United Nations Joint Human Rights Office (UNJHRO) revealed in a press release on November 24, 2025, that it had recorded 2,767 human rights violations and breaches of international humanitarian law in the Democratic Republic of Congo during the first half of the year, marking an 11% increase compared to the previous six months.

According to the report, 86% of these violations were concentrated in conflict-affected provinces, primarily resulting from the intensification of M23 offensives in North and South Kivu, as well as abuses committed by the ADF and CODECO in Ituri and North Kivu. The total number of victims in these areas reached 8,635, a 12% increase compared to the previous period.

The report details 416 violations in Ituri, a 21% increase over one year, including 198 abuses attributed to the ADF, responsible for at least 1,071 victims. Additionally, the UNJHRO highlighted the involvement of state agents in cases of sexual violence, affecting 70 victims, most of which were perpetrated by members of the FARDC.

title: South Kivu: At Least 12 Civilians Summarily Executed by M23 Fighters, NGO Reports
excerpt: Bukavu, DRC - The Pamoja kwa Amani coalition has sounded the alarm over a new wave of violence in South Kivu, reporting that at least 12 civilians were arrested and executed on the night of November 23-24, 2025 by…
title_en: South Kivu: At Least 12 Civilians Summarily Executed by M23 Fighters, NGO Reports
excerpt_en: Bukavu, DRC - The Pamoja kwa Amani coalition has sounded the alarm over a new wave of violence in South Kivu, reporting that at least 12 civilians were arrested and executed on the night of November 23-24, 2025 by…
body_en:
Bukavu, DRC - The Pamoja kwa Amani coalition has sounded the alarm over a new wave of violence in South Kivu, reporting that at least 12 civilians were arrested and executed on the night of November 23-24, 2025 by fighters from the AFC/M23 coalition in the Katana region of Kabare territory.

The victims, aged between 20 and 40, were accused of collaborating with the Wazalendo, allies of the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo). Among the dead was a patient forcibly taken from a health center before execution.

The NGO also documented other summary executions, including the killing and burial in a mass grave of two young men from the same family on November 21 in Kaniola, Walungu territory.

According to the Pamoja kwa Amani coalition, these acts, coupled with the dramatic escalation of violence, underscore the persistent severity of the security and humanitarian crisis in South Kivu, highlighting the urgent need for international attention and intervention to protect civilians.

title_en: North Kivu and Ituri: MONUSCO Reinforces Civilian Protection Amid Escalating Violence
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, DRC - Since early November 2025, MONUSCO peacekeepers have intensified their efforts to protect civilians in North Kivu and Ituri, conducting regular patrols, often jointly with the FARDC (Armed Forces of the…
body_en:
Kinshasa, DRC - Since early November 2025, MONUSCO peacekeepers have intensified their efforts to protect civilians in North Kivu and Ituri, conducting regular patrols, often jointly with the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo), to deter armed groups and strengthen local security.

According to Colonel Charles Idjiwa, an aerial reconnaissance mission was carried out on November 21 in the Mavivi-Mayangose Forest-Nyaleke triangle, in Beni, to improve intelligence gathering and coordination with the Congolese army.

In Ituri, a Nepalese civil engineering company rehabilitated 23 km of National Route 27, facilitating the movement of forces and civilians in sensitive areas.

In parallel, humanitarian and educational activities were organized in Bunia, benefiting nearly 500 students with educational games, hygiene awareness campaigns, and school supplies distribution, reinforcing the resilience of communities affected by the conflict.

title: Djugu: Baguru and Sesele Communities Strengthen Peaceful Coexistence in Ituri
excerpt: Djugu, Ituri - Over the past several weeks, peaceful coexistence between the Baguru and Sesele communities has been intensifying in the Djugu territory, following a series of meetings organized by political, military…
title_en: Djugu: Baguru and Sesele Communities Strengthen Peaceful Coexistence in Ituri
excerpt_en: Djugu, Ituri - Over the past several weeks, peaceful coexistence between the Baguru and Sesele communities has been intensifying in the Djugu territory, following a series of meetings organized by political, military…
body_en:
Djugu, Ituri - Over the past several weeks, peaceful coexistence between the Baguru and Sesele communities has been intensifying in the Djugu territory, following a series of meetings organized by political, military, and traditional authorities.

Local civil society, led by Gédéon Dino, welcomed the rapprochement, which was notably illustrated by a large gathering in Kpadole. This event brought together prominent figures, members of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), civil society actors, and representatives of the armed groups MAPI and CODECO, with the aim of promoting peaceful coexistence.

Earlier in November, traditional leaders of both communities also participated in a peace meeting in Tchomia, further strengthening dialogue. The results of these efforts are already visible with the resumption of activities in previously dangerous areas, such as the “La Morgue” gold mining site.

Local stakeholders are calling for this momentum to be maintained to ensure lasting peace in this part of the Djugu territory.

title: Uvira: 11 Dead in Two Days of Clashes Between FARDC and Wazalendo
excerpt: Uvira, South Kivu - Calm returned to Uvira on Tuesday, November 25, following two days of deadly clashes between the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and Wazalendo fighters.
title_en: Uvira: 11 Dead in Two Days of Clashes Between FARDC and Wazalendo
excerpt_en: Uvira, South Kivu - Calm returned to Uvira on Tuesday, November 25, following two days of deadly clashes between the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and Wazalendo fighters.
body_en:
Uvira, South Kivu - Calm returned to Uvira on Tuesday, November 25, following two days of deadly clashes between the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and Wazalendo fighters.

The death toll reached 11, with 4 wounded, including soldiers, Wazalendo fighters, and civilians caught in the crossfire. Hostilities began on Sunday, resulting in 9 deaths and 2 wounded, and continued on Monday, claiming 2 more lives and leaving 2 additional injured.

The clashes plunged the local population into a climate of trauma, despite the resumption of activities on Tuesday. Local sources report that the violence stems from a climate of mistrust and a power struggle between the two forces, which, despite their conflicts, are working together to contain the advance of the AFC-M23 rebellion toward Uvira, Tanganyika, and Haut-Katanga.

He reminded employers that the Congolese Labor Code - specifically Article 7, paragraph h, and Article 99 - guarantees regular remuneration, enabling workers to celebrate Christmas and New Year's with dignity.

Highlighting the government’s commitment to social protection, the Minister also announced the creation of an assistance program, effective January 6, 2026, to support workers who are victims of rights violations. This initiative aims to strengthen fairness, accountability, and compliance within Congolese businesses, ensuring that workers’ fundamental labor rights are respected.

The second half of November 2025 presents a stark dichotomy for the Democratic Republic of Congo: a nation making significant strides in international diplomacy and economic diversification, yet grappling with a deteriorating security crisis in its eastern provinces.

Security and Humanitarian Crisis Despite diplomatic efforts via the Washington and Doha processes, the security situation in eastern DRC remains critical. The ceasefire agreements have faced severe challenges, with the AFC/M23 coalition expanding its control in Masisi and South Kivu, establishing parallel administrations, and displacing thousands of civilians. The humanitarian toll is staggering, with over 19 million people in distress across the region and aid agencies facing financial constraints. While the FARDC has bolstered its capabilities through European Union funding and new military magistrate appointments, the persistent violence from armed groups like the ADF and M23 continues to be the deadliest threat to the population.

Diplomacy and Economic Diversification Conversely, Kinshasa has successfully pursued an aggressive strategy of economic diversification and international partnership. The period was marked by the signing of six major bilateral agreements with Qatar, including a $21 billion investment portfolio. Furthermore, the launch of a trade partnership with the United Kingdom and strengthened ties with Serbia signal a concerted effort to reduce reliance on raw mineral exports and boost local value chains. Domestically, the government’s 2026 draft budget reflects these priorities, allocating significant resources to security, infrastructure, and social protection.

Governance and Justice Internally, the DRC is navigating a complex political landscape. Tensions between provincial assemblies and executives have risen, evidenced by motions of censure in provinces like Mongala and Haut-Uele. However, the government has shown a firm commitment to justice and historical accountability, notably through the campaign for the recognition of the Congolese genocide, supported by religious denominations and African institutions. The swift prosecution in the Rawbank robbery case and the trial of armed groups in Walikale demonstrate a push to combat impunity and restore state authority.

Outlook As the DRC approaches the end of 2025, the nation stands at a pivotal crossroads. The immediate future will likely be defined by the government's ability to translate diplomatic and economic wins into tangible security improvements on the ground. All eyes will be on the upcoming high-level follow-up meeting scheduled for January 17, 2026, in Togo, which serves as a critical test for the consolidation of peace in the Great Lakes region.

title: Rwanda Confirms DRC Will Not Participate in Goma Airport Opening
excerpt: PARIS, FRANCE - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has confirmed that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government will not play a role in the upcoming opening of…
title_en: Rwanda Confirms DRC Will Not Participate in Goma Airport Opening
excerpt_en: PARIS, FRANCE - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has confirmed that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government will not play a role in the upcoming opening of…
body_en:
PARIS, FRANCE - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has confirmed that the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government will not play a role in the upcoming opening of Goma International Airport. The announcement follows a security meeting on the Great Lakes region held in Paris on October 30, 2025, where French President Emmanuel Macron revealed plans to open the airport in the coming weeks, with assistance from Qatar and the United States.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot explained that the Paris meeting aimed to accelerate discussions on Goma Airport’s reopening, with final decisions to be made in Doha, Qatar, between the AFC/M23 coalition and the DRC government. “This international conference was an opportunity to accelerate discussions on this issue, which will continue under the auspices of Qatar, with new information provided here in Paris,” Barrot said.

On November 1, DRC Government Spokesperson Patrick Muyaya stated that agencies responsible for airports and civil aviation have authority over Goma Airport. He claimed that if AFC/M23 controlled the airport, it would have been operational under their management since January. “Although they illegally control Goma airport, they have no right to decide which airports will be used,” Muyaya said.

Minister Nduhungirehe responded, emphasizing that France had clarified the decision to open Goma Airport would be made during the Doha talks. “Furthermore, the French proposal for opening Goma Airport does not involve the DRC government. Only MONUSCO and AFC/M23 will be involved,” he said.

President Macron has announced that once operational, Goma Airport will facilitate humanitarian flights twice a week.

title: Tshisekedi Repeats Claims That Rwanda Seeks to Annex Eastern Congo
excerpt: KINSHASA, DRC - President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi has once again accused Rwanda of seeking to annex parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), repeating claims that have repeatedly been denied by Kigali.
title_en: Tshisekedi Repeats Claims That Rwanda Seeks to Annex Eastern Congo
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, DRC - President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi has once again accused Rwanda of seeking to annex parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), repeating claims that have repeatedly been denied by Kigali.
body_en:
KINSHASA, DRC - President Félix Antoine Tshisekedi has once again accused Rwanda of seeking to annex parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), repeating claims that have repeatedly been denied by Kigali. Speaking to members of the Congolese diaspora in Egypt on Saturday, November 1, 2025, the Congolese leader alleged that Rwanda and President Paul Kagame have a “grand plan” to divide his country and seize its mineral-rich eastern provinces.

“His goal is to divide our country and occupy it, and even annex the eastern part, which has land rich in minerals and agriculture,” Tshisekedi told the audience in Cairo.

Rwanda has consistently rejected such allegations, insisting that its actions are driven solely by security concerns and not by any desire to claim Congolese territory or resources.

In a March 2025 interview, President Kagame reaffirmed that Rwanda’s primary focus is national security, not access to the DRC’s natural wealth. “If you look at the list of hundreds of companies from around the world - China, Europe, America, Canada, and others - that are interested in Congo’s minerals, Rwanda would be in 100th place, at the very end,” Kagame said in an interview with journalist Mario Nawfall.

He added that discussions about minerals are misplaced, emphasizing that “it is impossible for Rwanda, without first securing its long-term stability, to think about minerals. That would be the last thing we would think about.”

President Tshisekedi also claimed that President Kagame was responsible for the failure of the Luanda peace talks, alleging that the Rwandan leader refused to attend the signing ceremony. Kigali, however, has rejected that account.

In January 2025, President Kagame stated that he had withdrawn from the meeting due to what he described as “inappropriate behavior” from the DRC delegation. Despite this, both nations have maintained a formal peace agreement - though tensions remain high along the border.

Tshisekedi’s renewed accusations come at a delicate time, as he and President Kagame are expected to meet soon in Washington, D.C., for talks hosted by U.S. President Donald Trump. The meeting aims to promote peace and strengthen economic cooperation between Kigali and Kinshasa.

Observers warn that Tshisekedi’s latest remarks risk undermining those efforts. His continued rhetoric against Rwanda, despite recent diplomatic progress, has raised questions about his commitment to reconciliation and regional stability.

title: Rwanda Dismisses Tshisekedi’s Claims of Annexation Ambitions, Cites Corruption in Katanga
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has firmly rejected accusations by Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi that Rwanda…
title_en: Rwanda Dismisses Tshisekedi’s Claims of Annexation Ambitions, Cites Corruption in Katanga
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has firmly rejected accusations by Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi that Rwanda…
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has firmly rejected accusations by Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi that Rwanda seeks to annex part of Congolese territory. The remarks come amid escalating rhetoric between the two neighboring nations, whose relations remain tense over ongoing insecurity in eastern DRC.

During a meeting with members of the Congolese diaspora in Egypt on November 2, 2025, President Tshisekedi alleged that Rwanda covets the mineral-rich eastern region of his country, claiming Kigali’s motives are driven by a desire to control its natural resources and fertile land.

In response, Minister Nduhungirehe dismissed the allegations as “baseless and ironic,” turning the accusation back on Tshisekedi himself. “If I have followed the news correctly,” he said on November 3, “it is the Tshisekedi family that wants to ‘keep’ the natural resources of Katanga in its coffers.”

Rwandan officials have repeatedly maintained that their country has no territorial or economic ambitions in the DRC. President Paul Kagame has consistently emphasized that Rwanda’s primary concern is its national security - particularly the threat posed by armed groups operating near its borders.

In a March 2025 address, Kagame underscored that Rwanda’s interest in the DRC’s resources is minimal compared to that of global mining corporations. “If you look at the list of hundreds of companies from China, Europe, America, Canada and others that are involved in Congo’s minerals, Rwanda would come 100th - at the very end,” he said.

The exchange of accusations comes as members of President Tshisekedi’s family face growing scrutiny over alleged involvement in mineral theft and corruption in the Katanga and Lualaba regions - areas that produce a significant share of the world’s copper and cobalt.

Local residents and industry sources have accused the Tshisekedi family, including the president’s brother Christian Tshisekedi, of turning Katanga into a personal “cash cow” by extracting vast mineral wealth without reinvesting in the province.

“Since 2019, Katanga has become the Tshisekedi family’s cash cow,” one Katanga resident told reporters. “They extract wealth from the province, especially Lualaba, but invest nothing back.”

Reports from mining groups indicate that security forces, including members of the Republican Guard, have been deployed to certain mining sites to facilitate illegal extraction and transport of minerals.

In response to these allegations, Katanga’s regional authorities have retained Belgian lawyer Bernard Maingain to initiate legal proceedings against Christian Tshisekedi and his associates in both the DRC and Belgium, where they reportedly hold dual citizenship.

“We plan to file complaints in the DRC and in Belgium,” Maingain said, adding that the case involves “serious crimes of corruption, embezzlement, and the illegal use of funds.”

On October 28, DRC Minister of Justice Guillaume Ngefa announced that the National Commission for Combating Illegal Mining (CNLFM) had completed an investigation implicating several civilians, soldiers, police officers, and foreign nationals in large-scale mineral theft. Ngefa instructed the Prosecutor’s Office to pursue legal action against all those identified, regardless of their rank or nationality.

While the report’s findings have not been made public, it remains unclear whether members of the Tshisekedi family are among those named - a revelation that could have far-reaching political consequences.

The latest exchange between Kinshasa and Kigali reflects deepening mistrust between the two countries, whose strained relations have been marked by mutual accusations over security and resource exploitation.As both governments trade allegations of corruption and aggression, regional observers warn that the escalating war of words could further destabilize the Great Lakes region if diplomacy fails to prevail.

title: Rwanda, Egypt Strengthen Cooperation During GEM Opening
excerpt: CAIRO, EGYPT - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe, met with his Egyptian counterpart, Dr. Badr Abdelatty, to discuss ways to deepen cooperation between the two countries across multiple sectors.
title_en: Rwanda, Egypt Strengthen Cooperation During GEM Opening
excerpt_en: CAIRO, EGYPT - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe, met with his Egyptian counterpart, Dr. Badr Abdelatty, to discuss ways to deepen cooperation between the two countries across multiple sectors.
body_en:
CAIRO, EGYPT - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe, met with his Egyptian counterpart, Dr. Badr Abdelatty, to discuss ways to deepen cooperation between the two countries across multiple sectors. The meeting took place during the opening of the Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM) on November 1, 2025, which Minister Nduhungirehe attended as part of Rwanda’s diplomatic delegation.

Minister Nduhungirehe thanked Egypt for hosting the opening ceremony and reaffirmed Rwanda’s commitment to continue strengthening bilateral relations.

Grand Egyptian Museum: A Global Cultural Landmark

The GEM, the world’s largest museum, houses over 100,000 artifacts tracing Egypt’s 7,000-year history. Construction began in 2005 on a 50-hectare site near the Giza pyramids at a cost exceeding $1 billion. Visitors are greeted by an 11-meter-tall, eight-ton statue of Pharaoh Ramesses II, with staircases leading to statues of ancient kings and queens.

The museum is divided into three sections - social, royal, and religious life - showcasing historical changes over millennia. Among its highlights are King Khufu’s ship, temples known as ‘naos,’ statues of Egyptian gods like Osiris and Ptah, and a children’s education section with a library of historical documents. The museum also features a comprehensive display of Tutankhamun Nebkheperure’s artifacts, including 5,398 objects arranged in 7,500 square meters, presented together for the first time.

Rwanda and Egypt have steadily developed diplomatic and economic ties. On September 28, 2025, both countries signed a visa exchange agreement during the UN General Assembly in New York. Earlier in October, President Paul Kagame visited Egypt, meeting President Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi and signing agreements on investment promotion, water management, land exchanges, and urban development.

Bilateral agreements signed in August 2024 cover health, transport, trade, and other sectors, complemented by ongoing collaboration in technology, industrial and commercial development, agriculture, education, youth, health, and military cooperation.

Diplomatic relations between the two countries date back decades. Egypt has maintained an embassy in Kigali since 1976, and Rwanda reopened its embassy in Cairo in March 2015. The 2017 visit of President Al-Sisi to Rwanda further strengthened the long-standing partnership.

title: Rwanda’s Foreign Minister Criticizes MONUSCO as 'One of UN’s Greatest Failures'
excerpt: KIGALI, Rwanda - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has sharply criticized the United Nations peacekeeping mission in the Democratic Republic of the…
title_en: Rwanda’s Foreign Minister Criticizes MONUSCO as 'One of UN’s Greatest Failures'
excerpt_en: KIGALI, Rwanda - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has sharply criticized the United Nations peacekeeping mission in the Democratic Republic of the…
body_en:
KIGALI, Rwanda - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has sharply criticized the United Nations peacekeeping mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), calling it “one of the greatest failures in the history of the United Nations.”

In a statement issued on November 5, 2025, Minister Nduhungirehe condemned the mission for training DRC government forces (FARDC) to use heavy weapons and drones-equipment he said has been used to violate ceasefire agreements and target civilians in eastern Congo.

“If I understand correctly, MONUSCO’s primary responsibility is to protect civilians,” Nduhungirehe said. “Yet it is training the DRC army-which is working alongside the genocidal FDLR group-to use weapons and drones that are being used daily to attack civilians.”

The criticism followed remarks by Lt. Gen. Johnny Luboya N’Kashama, Governor of Ituri Province, who said the ongoing exercises would help DRC soldiers become “more professional” and “defeat the enemy.”

Minister Nduhungirehe, however, argued that MONUSCO’s actions undermine its mandate, enabling government forces to continue hostilities against the AFC/M23 coalition in violation of the ceasefire.

Despite being deployed in the DRC for over 25 years and spending nearly $20 billion, MONUSCO has failed to stabilize the volatile eastern regions, where more than 16,000 peacekeepers are still stationed.

Nduhungirehe further accused the mission of allowing armed groups like the FDLR to rebuild, while hate speech and persecution against Kinyarwanda-speaking communities continue unchecked.

His remarks add to a growing chorus of regional voices questioning the effectiveness and accountability of UN peacekeeping operations in the Great Lakes region.

title: Ambassador Busingye Joins Britons in Honoring War Heroes
excerpt: LONDON, United Kingdom - Rwanda’s High Commissioner to the United Kingdom, Ambassador Johnston Busingye, on Sunday, November 9, 2025, joined the people of Britain in commemorating those who lost their lives in the First…
title_en: Ambassador Busingye Joins Britons in Honoring War Heroes
excerpt_en: LONDON, United Kingdom - Rwanda’s High Commissioner to the United Kingdom, Ambassador Johnston Busingye, on Sunday, November 9, 2025, joined the people of Britain in commemorating those who lost their lives in the First…
body_en:
LONDON, United Kingdom - Rwanda’s High Commissioner to the United Kingdom, Ambassador Johnston Busingye, on Sunday, November 9, 2025, joined the people of Britain in commemorating those who lost their lives in the First and Second World Wars and subsequent conflicts.

The solemn ceremony, held at Whitehall in London, brought together national leaders, diplomats, and citizens to pay tribute to the fallen. Among those in attendance were King Charles III, Prime Minister Keir Starmer, and members of the diplomatic corps, including Ambassador Busingye.

Similar remembrance services were also held across the United Kingdom - in Edinburgh, Belfast, and Cardiff - as part of the country’s annual Remembrance Sunday tradition. The commemoration included the laying of wreaths at the Cenotaph monument and a two-minute silence to honor the memory of soldiers who perished in both world wars and other military operations.

Around 10,000 former servicemen and women, including 20 veterans of World War II, took part in the ceremony, which was marked by a moving display of national pride and reflection.

The United Kingdom observes Remembrance Sunday each year on the second Sunday of November, in conjunction with Armistice Day on November 11 - the date marking the end of World War I in 1918. This year’s commemoration carried special significance, coinciding with the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II.

Prime Minister Keir Starmer paid tribute to the courage and sacrifice of the armed forces, emphasizing their enduring legacy. “Today we remember the extraordinary sacrifices made by our military in the war and the conflicts that followed,” he said. “Their actions have helped us achieve the freedom we enjoy today.”

During both World Wars, Britain fought on the victorious side but paid a heavy price. The country lost an estimated 886,000 soldiers in World War I and 384,000 in World War II.

Ambassador Busingye’s participation underscores Rwanda’s solidarity with Commonwealth nations in honoring shared histories of service, sacrifice, and resilience.

title: Ambassador Nzabamwita Highlights Rwanda’s Energy Transformation, Calls for Stronger Cooperation with Russia
excerpt: Moscow, Russia - Rwanda’s Ambassador to Russia, Joseph Nzabamwita, has highlighted Rwanda’s remarkable progress in expanding energy access and urged deeper cooperation between Rwanda and Russia in the energy sector.
title_en: Ambassador Nzabamwita Highlights Rwanda’s Energy Transformation, Calls for Stronger Cooperation with Russia
excerpt_en: Moscow, Russia - Rwanda’s Ambassador to Russia, Joseph Nzabamwita, has highlighted Rwanda’s remarkable progress in expanding energy access and urged deeper cooperation between Rwanda and Russia in the energy sector.
body_en:
Moscow, Russia - Rwanda’s Ambassador to Russia, Joseph Nzabamwita, has highlighted Rwanda’s remarkable progress in expanding energy access and urged deeper cooperation between Rwanda and Russia in the energy sector.

Speaking in an interview with Maxim Zakharov during Russian Energy Week, Ambassador Nzabamwita reflected on Rwanda’s transformation over the past decade and its ambitions for sustainable energy development.

“Rwanda went from having 6% of its population with access to electricity in 2009 to 84.6% today,” he said. “You see, from 6% to 84.6% - a lot of work has been done, but we are not where we want to be.”

Nzabamwita emphasized that Rwanda’s progress is a source of national pride, reflecting years of investment in infrastructure, innovation, and renewable energy. Under Vision 2050, the country aims to generate 50% of its electricity from renewable sources, which he noted are now the most cost-effective and sustainable energy options available.

He said Rwanda’s strategy includes mobilizing citizens to adopt renewable energy technologies and strengthening international partnerships to improve efficiency and diversify sources.

Rwanda and Russia signed a nuclear energy cooperation agreement in 2018, and Nzabamwita expressed hope that such collaboration will continue to expand. “Rwanda can learn a lot from Russia because it has been a country that has been producing energy for many years, and Rwanda needs to know how to find the energy it needs as a developing country,” he said.

Beyond energy, the ambassador pointed to growing cooperation between the two countries in education and cultural exchange. He noted that more Rwandan students are pursuing studies in Russia, while Russian students and scholars have increasingly engaged in academic programs and study visits to Rwanda.

“There are many things that connect Rwanda and Russia,” Nzabamwita said. “Some universities, such as St. Petersburg State University, have even introduced courses in Kinyarwanda and Swahili, reflecting the deepening ties between our peoples.”

The ambassador concluded by reaffirming Rwanda’s commitment to strengthening partnerships that promote innovation, sustainability, and mutual growth across key sectors, including energy and education.

title: Unity and Reconciliation Among Rwandans Reach 95.3% in 2025 - Minister Bizimana
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda - Rwanda’s unity and reconciliation rate has reached 95.3% in 2025, according to findings announced by Dr. Jean Damascène Bizimana, Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement.
title_en: Unity and Reconciliation Among Rwandans Reach 95.3% in 2025 - Minister Bizimana
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda - Rwanda’s unity and reconciliation rate has reached 95.3% in 2025, according to findings announced by Dr. Jean Damascène Bizimana, Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement.
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda - Rwanda’s unity and reconciliation rate has reached 95.3% in 2025, according to findings announced by Dr. Jean Damascène Bizimana, Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement. The figures come from a national survey on unity, reconciliation, and sustainability conducted every five years by the National Unity and Reconciliation Commission (NURC).

In 2020, the national reconciliation rate stood at 94.7%, showing continued progress over the past five years. The 2025 survey covered 12,300 participants - including 8,100 households and 4,200 institutions - and consisted of 123 questions aimed at capturing a comprehensive picture of Rwanda’s social cohesion.

Of the respondents, 52% were women and 48% men. Youth under 35 represented 47%, while 53% were older. Educational backgrounds varied: 38% had completed primary education, 26% secondary, 14% university, 2% vocational, while 21% had no formal education.

In terms of faith, the majority identified as Catholics (41%), followed by ADEPR (24%), Adventists (12%), Anglicans (8%), Presbyterians (3%), Muslims (3%), Methodists (2%), Baptists (2%), Jehovah’s Witnesses (1%), and non-religious (1%).

Sustainability at 90.8%.

Among the most influential factors promoting national unity were courage and patriotism (98.7%), traditional values and beliefs (97.9%), sense of belonging (96%), and shared national values (95.9%). Respondents also cited lessons learned from the Genocide against the Tutsi (92.6%) and the failure of divisive political parties before 1994 (91.9%) as key motivators for unity.

For reconciliation, the strongest pillars included good interpersonal relations (98.5%), personal freedom and belonging (95.9%), shared historical understanding (90.6%), and the importance of remembrance of the Genocide against the Tutsi (99%).

An overwhelming 100% of respondents said they are proud to be Rwandan, with Kinyarwanda cited as the backbone of national identity.Other highlights include:

98% believe there is political will to build unity;

98% are proud of Rwanda’s national heroes;

98% consider Itorero and Ndi Umunyarwanda civic education programs effective;

99% agree that the Genocide was planned;

97% view Rwandanness as the most important identity;

97% believe the current leadership governs without ethnic discrimination;

96% support teaching history to the youth;

93% say all Rwandans have equal access to national opportunities.

Despite the progress, challenges persist.

23% of respondents acknowledged that traces of the Genocide ideology still exist in their communities.

38% believe some Genocide perpetrators remain attached to divisive beliefs.

34% think certain ex-prisoners who served sentences still harbor hatred.

40% view foreign-based social media platforms as harmful to national unity.

32% admitted lacking awareness about civic responsibility.

45% of Genocide survivors reported that they still carry psychological wounds.

The Eastern Province led the unity index at 97.2%, followed by:

City of Kigali (93.7%).

Top-performing districts included Kayonza, Ngoma, Ruhango, Nyanza, and Kirehe, while Gisagara, Rulindo, Huye, Nyarugenge, and Rusizi ranked lower.

Minister Dr. Bizimana emphasized the need to strengthen unity programs, particularly among the youth. He called for renewed efforts to:

Expand education on Rwandan cultural values, history, and the Kinyarwanda language;

Encourage youth participation in unity-building activities starting from the family level;

Combat Genocide ideology domestically and abroad; and

Promote national cohesion programs among the Rwandan diaspora.

He concluded by reaffirming the government’s commitment to ensuring that Rwandan unity remains strong, inclusive, and enduring for generations to come.

title: President Kagame Recognized for Promoting Literature in Africa
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda - The Pan African Movement Rwanda (PAM) has expressed gratitude to President Paul Kagame for his significant contributions to promoting literature across Africa.
title_en: President Kagame Recognized for Promoting Literature in Africa
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda - The Pan African Movement Rwanda (PAM) has expressed gratitude to President Paul Kagame for his significant contributions to promoting literature across Africa.
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda - The Pan African Movement Rwanda (PAM) has expressed gratitude to President Paul Kagame for his significant contributions to promoting literature across Africa. The recognition came during celebrations for World Writers’ Day on November 7, 2025, which also saw awards presented to institutions and individuals advancing the culture of reading and writing.

PAM highlighted President Kagame’s efforts to encourage reading, support writers focusing on African history, and engage in broader educational initiatives that foster a culture of literature on the continent. Among the award recipients was the Ministry of Defense, recognized as a government institution that has helped writers develop and promote literary culture.

The Deputy Director of PAM in Rwanda, Twagirimana Epimaque, noted that while the culture of reading has grown, challenges remain due to the lack of a regulatory framework for writers.

“We are calling for a policy to be put in place to regulate book writing because, to date, there are no fixed rules governing book writing. This makes it difficult for writers to find the means and resources to write, even when the ideas are there,” he said.

Hategekimana Richard, Director General of the Rwandan Writers’ Guild and recipient of the Best Writer of the Year award, emphasized that the culture of writing should not be confined to universities and higher education institutions but should also reach primary school children.

“Children also read and should learn how books are written and produced. This encourages a love for writing from a young age,” he said, noting that children’s reading and writing competitions have been established to cultivate this culture.

Dr. Baguma Rose, Director of the Department of Education Policy at MINEDUC, stressed the foundational role of books in education.

“Books are the primary teaching aids, from children to adults. Writing is crucial for improving the quality of education because written knowledge supports innovation and helps us understand our history and identity,” she said.

During the ceremony, 12 awards were presented, including recognitions for:

Universities promoting reading in schools and communities

The event highlighted Rwanda’s ongoing commitment to developing a reading and writing culture, ensuring that literature remains a vital tool for education, knowledge, and national identity.

title: Tshisekedi Signals Imminent “Final Deal” Between DRC and Rwanda
excerpt: Brasília, Brazil - President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has indicated that his country’s “final” peace and cooperation agreement with Rwanda will be signed in the coming days.
title_en: Tshisekedi Signals Imminent “Final Deal” Between DRC and Rwanda
excerpt_en: Brasília, Brazil - President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has indicated that his country’s “final” peace and cooperation agreement with Rwanda will be signed in the coming days.
body_en:
Brasília, Brazil - President Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has indicated that his country’s “final” peace and cooperation agreement with Rwanda will be signed in the coming days. He made the announcement during a meeting with Congolese citizens in Brazil on November 7, 2025, signaling the conclusion of long-standing diplomatic talks.

Tshisekedi confirmed that both the Doha and Washington negotiations are expected to reach a positive conclusion shortly.

“I am pleased to inform you that the Doha and Washington talks will have a positive conclusion in the coming days,” he said.

The United States has described the forthcoming economic cooperation agreement as the “last” such deal between Rwanda and the DRC. The signing ceremony is expected to be attended by President Paul Kagame of Rwanda and President Tshisekedi.

The agreement aims to promote peace and sustainable development in the region and will follow the completion of a peace deal between the DRC government and the AFC/M23 coalition, facilitated with support from Qatar, which has been leading the Doha talks.

President Tshisekedi added that the White House will soon send official invitations to both countries for the signing.

“In the coming days, the White House will send us an invitation to sign the peace agreement,” he said.

On the same day, Rwanda and the DRC finalized the full draft of the economic cooperation agreement, which the United States hailed as a significant step toward implementing the long-awaited accord.

The deal represents a major milestone in stabilizing relations between the two neighboring countries and advancing regional economic and security cooperation.

title: President Kagame Hosts U.S. Faith Advisors to Discuss Peace and Governance
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda - President Paul Kagame and First Lady Jeannette Kagame welcomed Paula White-Cain, Advisor to the President of the United States on Faith Affairs, and Jenny Korn, Director of the White House Faith Office…
title_en: President Kagame Hosts U.S. Faith Advisors to Discuss Peace and Governance
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda - President Paul Kagame and First Lady Jeannette Kagame welcomed Paula White-Cain, Advisor to the President of the United States on Faith Affairs, and Jenny Korn, Director of the White House Faith Office…
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda - President Paul Kagame and First Lady Jeannette Kagame welcomed Paula White-Cain, Advisor to the President of the United States on Faith Affairs, and Jenny Korn, Director of the White House Faith Office, for discussions on peace, faith, governance, and regional issues.

The meeting focused on matters of mutual concern for Rwanda, the region, and the global community. White-Cain and Korn are part of the White House Faith Office, established in 2025 by President Donald Trump to promote faith-based values in families and safeguard religious freedom. The office operates under the Office of Counsel and Strategy within the U.S. President’s administration and collaborates with other faith-based organizations globally.

Other attendees included Bradley Knight, Bishop Nicholas Duncan-Williams, Rosa Whitaker Duncan-Williams, Joel Duncan-Williams, and Chekinah Olivier.

On the Rwandan side, the discussions were joined by Dr. Jean Damascène Bizimana, Minister of National Unity, and Nelly Mukazayire, Minister of Sports.

The meeting underscores Rwanda’s commitment to faith, governance, and peacebuilding, while strengthening ties with international partners engaged in promoting values-based leadership and social cohesion.

title: Rwanda Absent as DRC Hosts Great Lakes Summit Amid Ongoing Tensions
excerpt: Kinshasa, DRC - Rwanda was notably absent from the Great Lakes Region Heads of State Summit hosted by the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), despite being a member of the regional bloc.
title_en: Rwanda Absent as DRC Hosts Great Lakes Summit Amid Ongoing Tensions
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, DRC - Rwanda was notably absent from the Great Lakes Region Heads of State Summit hosted by the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), despite being a member of the regional bloc.
body_en:
Kinshasa, DRC - Rwanda was notably absent from the Great Lakes Region Heads of State Summit hosted by the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), despite being a member of the regional bloc. The meeting, scheduled for November 15, 2025, is expected to focus heavily on the deteriorating security situation in eastern DRC.

A senior Rwandan official cited two main reasons for Kigali’s absence: “security issues are not in order” and President Paul Kagame did not receive a direct invitation from his Congolese counterpart, President Félix Tshisekedi. Reports indicate that the only communication sent to Rwanda came through a letter from the DRC Embassy in Ethiopia, which Kigali did not consider an official invitation.

The summit brought together four of the nine heads of state from the Great Lakes Region:

Evariste Ndayishimiye (Burundi) alongside the host, President Félix Tshisekedi.

Rwanda’s absence underscores the deep strain in relations between the two neighbors, whose ties have sharply deteriorated over allegations of mutual support to armed groups operating around the eastern DRC.

The Great Lakes Region bloc is part of the regional mediation mechanism tasked with monitoring the ceasefire agreement signed in October 2025 between the DRC government and the AFC/M23 coalition during negotiations held in Doha.

However, the truce has never taken hold. The FARDC has continued conducting military operations-including the use of drones and heavy artillery-in areas controlled by the AFC/M23 and communities of the Banyamulenge, despite regional and international calls for restraint.

The continued clashes have raised concerns that the absence of a key regional player like Rwanda could further undermine efforts to stabilize eastern DRC, as diplomatic channels between Kigali and Kinshasa remain strained.

The summit brought together four of the nine heads of state from the Great Lakes Region:

Evariste Ndayishimiye (Burundi) alongside the host, President Félix Tshisekedi.

Rwanda’s absence underscores the deep strain in relations between the two neighbors, whose ties have sharply deteriorated over allegations of mutual support to armed groups operating around the eastern DRC.

The Great Lakes Region bloc is part of the regional mediation mechanism tasked with monitoring the ceasefire agreement signed in October 2025 between the DRC government and the AFC/M23 coalition during negotiations held in Doha.

However, the truce has never taken hold. The FARDC has continued conducting military operations-including the use of drones and heavy artillery-in areas controlled by the AFC/M23 and communities of the Banyamulenge, despite regional and international calls for restraint.

The continued clashes have raised concerns that the absence of a key regional player like Rwanda could further undermine efforts to stabilize eastern DRC, as diplomatic channels between Kigali and Kinshasa remain strained.

title: DRC Government and AFC/M23 Sign Principles Framework Toward Lasting Peace
excerpt: Doha, Qatar - The Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 coalition have taken a significant step toward ending years of conflict in eastern Congo, signing a set of eight guiding principles…
title_en: DRC Government and AFC/M23 Sign Principles Framework Toward Lasting Peace
excerpt_en: Doha, Qatar - The Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 coalition have taken a significant step toward ending years of conflict in eastern Congo, signing a set of eight guiding principles…
body_en:
Doha, Qatar - The Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 coalition have taken a significant step toward ending years of conflict in eastern Congo, signing a set of eight guiding principles designed to address the root causes of the crisis and pave the way for a comprehensive peace agreement.

The document was signed on November 15, 2025, in Doha, where negotiations have been facilitated by Qatar with support from the United States.

Benjamin Mbonimpa, Permanent Secretary of the AFC/M23, said the agreement outlines a structured roadmap for the peace process, with each principle to be discussed in detail under a predetermined timetable. Only after the issues under all eight principles are resolved, he said, will both parties proceed to signing a final, holistic peace agreement.

“There will be no change in the site or operations until these principles are fully discussed and a final decision is reached on the general peace agreement,” Mbonimpa said. “Our people, please be patient-the journey is still long.”

The signed framework includes the following core commitments:

Restoration of State Authority in Eastern DRC: Government institutions and public services are to be progressively re-established in the east, implemented jointly by the DRC Government and the AFC/M23.

Interim Security Measures: Both sides agreed to adopt temporary security arrangements aimed at maintaining public order and protecting civilians during the transition period.

Creation of a National Truth and Reconciliation Commission: The parties will establish an independent body mandated to uncover the truth about past abuses, promote reconciliation, investigate crimes, and outline mechanisms for reparations.

The signing ceremony was attended by Dr. Mohammed bin Abdulaziz bin Saleh Al-Khulaifi, Qatar’s Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, and Massad Boulos, the U.S. Presidential Advisor for African Affairs.

Boulos welcomed the progress but cautioned that substantial work remains before a definitive peace agreement can be concluded.

“It will take time, but not too long,” he said, urging continued commitment from both sides.

The principles agreement marks one of the most significant diplomatic developments in the DRC conflict in years, though the ultimate success of the process will depend on sustained compliance, trust-building, and the ability of both parties to implement the roadmap on the ground.

title: Rwanda, UNIDO and Poland Launch Partnership to Strengthen Disaster Risk Reduction
excerpt: Vienna, Austria - November 12, 2025 - Rwanda, the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), and the Government of Poland have launched a new partnership aimed at boosting Rwanda’s capacity to prevent…
title_en: Rwanda, UNIDO and Poland Launch Partnership to Strengthen Disaster Risk Reduction
excerpt_en: Vienna, Austria - November 12, 2025 - Rwanda, the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), and the Government of Poland have launched a new partnership aimed at boosting Rwanda’s capacity to prevent…
body_en:
Vienna, Austria - November 12, 2025 - Rwanda, the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), and the Government of Poland have launched a new partnership aimed at boosting Rwanda’s capacity to prevent and respond to industrial and climate-related disasters.

The agreement, signed Wednesday at UNIDO headquarters in Vienna, formalizes a project funded by Poland and implemented by UNIDO in collaboration with Rwanda’s Ministry of Internal Security through the Rwanda Police Fire & Rescue Brigade.

UNIDO Director-General Gerd Müller, Rwanda’s Permanent Representative to the UN Ambassador Urujeni Bakuramutsa, and Poland’s Representative to UNIDO Ambassador Marek Szczygieł, together with officials from Poland’s Ministry of Economic Development and Technology, signed the cooperation framework.

Müller described the initiative as the start of a “tripartite partnership,” bringing together Poland as a new donor, UNIDO’s technological expertise, and Rwanda’s drive toward disaster-resilient development.

“Today is not just a signing of a document, but the beginning of a three-way partnership,” Müller said. “Together, we will find practical solutions that will improve people’s lives and build a better and more sustainable future.”

The project aims to strengthen institutional capabilities, enhance research on disaster risks and impacts, and support the development of improved response mechanisms. A second phase will focus on capacity building and the provision of specialized firefighting equipment.

Ambassador Bakuramutsa said the initiative reflects Rwanda’s commitment to international cooperation aligned with the country’s development priorities.

“This project is closely linked to the implementation of our NST2 and Vision 2050, particularly in building an economy rooted in modern and environmentally friendly industries,” she said.

Poland’s Ambassador Szczygieł highlighted his country’s growing engagement in development cooperation with African nations, citing previous collaborations with UNIDO in Tajikistan, Moldova, and Georgia.

“This project is a concrete example of Poland’s commitment to development cooperation with African countries,” he said.

The partners envision establishing a long-term cooperation model focused on disaster risk reduction, innovation, and industrial development.

title: Rwanda Calls for Shift From Military Power to Political Dialogue in UN Peacekeeping
excerpt: New York - Rwanda has reiterated its long-standing position that effective peacekeeping must prioritize political solutions over military strength.
title_en: Rwanda Calls for Shift From Military Power to Political Dialogue in UN Peacekeeping
excerpt_en: New York - Rwanda has reiterated its long-standing position that effective peacekeeping must prioritize political solutions over military strength.
body_en:
New York - Rwanda has reiterated its long-standing position that effective peacekeeping must prioritize political solutions over military strength. Speaking before the UN General Assembly’s Fourth Committee (Special Political and Decolonization), Colonel Deo Mutabazi, Head of Military Operations at the Rwandan Embassy to the United Nations, argued that durable peace cannot be achieved through force alone.

Col. Mutabazi said the international community has traditionally assumed that protecting civilians requires large and heavily equipped military missions, but this approach has repeatedly proven insufficient.

“We believe that no capacity, technology, or even training can better protect civilians than investing in finding ways to achieve peace through political dialogue,” he said. “This is where many UN peacekeeping missions remain weak.”

He stressed that addressing the root causes of conflict - including mismanagement, corruption, inequality, discrimination, and poverty - is essential for sustainable peace. Military force, he noted, cannot resolve problems that are fundamentally political.

Col. Mutabazi also criticized the mismatch between the mandates of some UN peacekeeping missions and the realities on the ground. At times, he said, mission responsibilities contradict what is actually needed, leading to tensions with host countries and even making peacekeepers targets for local populations.

He warned that such contradictions often emerge when missions attempt to resolve political crises through military means, despite the availability of peaceful alternatives.

“It is time to rethink how peacekeeping mandates are designed,” he added, arguing that decisions dominated by powerful countries have created missions “like Christmas trees” - overloaded with tasks that benefit external actors more than the host nation.

Col. Mutabazi called for stronger collaboration between the UN and regional organizations, saying that troops deployed under continental or regional frameworks have demonstrated their ability to restore stability and create space for peacebuilding.

He also highlighted troubling cases where UN peacekeepers have been drawn into local conflicts or, in some instances, have cooperated with illegal armed groups. To prevent such situations, he said, peacekeeping responsibilities must be clearly aligned with international law.

The Rwandan officer emphasized that one of the most cost-effective approaches to strengthening peace is deep community engagement. Programs that link peacekeepers with local leaders and residents - especially through activities in health, sanitation, environmental protection, and school rehabilitation - create trust and open channels of communication.

“Our experience has shown that working with communities produces positive results and helps combat misinformation and hate speech,” he said. “It builds genuine relationships between communities, their leaders, and peacekeepers.”

Rwanda’s Defence Forces have long used this model in their peacekeeping deployments, often participating in community activities such as cleaning campaigns, health interventions, and school construction or renovation. According to Mutabazi, these efforts help peacekeepers and local populations “feel like brothers,” strengthening cooperation and security.

title: New Date Sought for Kagame-Tshisekedi Meeting in Washington After U.S. Postponement
excerpt: A new date is being negotiated for the high-level meeting between Rwandan President Paul Kagame and Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi in Washington, D.C., after the United States…
title_en: New Date Sought for Kagame-Tshisekedi Meeting in Washington After U.S. Postponement
excerpt_en: A new date is being negotiated for the high-level meeting between Rwandan President Paul Kagame and Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi in Washington, D.C., after the United States…
body_en:
A new date is being negotiated for the high-level meeting between Rwandan President Paul Kagame and Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi in Washington, D.C., after the United States postponed the scheduled encounter of November 13, 2025.

The two leaders had been expected to meet with U.S. President Donald Trump for the signing of an economic development partnership agreement, designed to reinforce the peace accord Rwanda and the DRC concluded on June 27, 2025.

Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, confirmed on November 12 that both presidents had agreed to attend the talks before Washington abruptly delayed them.

"President Tshisekedi, like President Kagame, had agreed to attend the Washington meeting scheduled for November 13, before the U.S. government postponed it at the last minute," Nduhungirehe said. "The three parties are now looking for another date that fits their schedules."

DRC government spokesman Patrick Muyaya told Radio France Internationale (RFI) that President Tshisekedi would only travel to Washington once Rwandan troops withdraw from eastern Congo.

Kigali has repeatedly rejected claims of troop deployment, insisting it has only reinforced its border to prevent incursions by the FDLR and other armed groups operating in eastern DRC.

Nduhungirehe dismissed Muyaya’s statements, accusing him of deliberately misleading the public. He stressed that all parties had already agreed the Washington meeting would focus on finalizing and signing a bilateral economic cooperation agreement.

The draft agreement-approved by Rwandan and Congolese delegations on November 7-covers collaboration in key sectors such as mining, the joint construction of the Rusizi III hydroelectric dam, and cross-border trade facilitation.

President Trump has publicly stated several times that the economic pact would boost prosperity and stability in both countries and deliver broader regional benefits.

On July 9, he told reporters that Kagame and Tshisekedi were expected to meet in Washington “in the next few weeks” to sign what he described as “the final agreement.”

Despite U.S. assurances, persistent tensions between Kigali and Kinshasa have repeatedly jeopardized scheduling efforts.

Three months after Trump’s initial announcement, Washington again attempted to bring the two leaders together on October 23. However, within 20 days, the DRC government declared it would not sign any economic accord until security issues were resolved.

Subsequent talks led the U.S. to postpone the meeting to November 13, but that date also collapsed-this time without explanation.

According to Africa Intelligence, U.S. officials are now attempting to reschedule the meeting for November 21, following multiple unsuccessful attempts to convene the two presidents.
