title: RGB Explains Closure of Over 9,000 Churches and Mosques in Rwanda
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda - The Rwanda Governance Board (RGB) has provided clarification on the closure of 9,171 churches and mosques across the country, citing non-compliance with legal and governance requirements.
title_en: RGB Explains Closure of Over 9,000 Churches and Mosques in Rwanda
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda - The Rwanda Governance Board (RGB) has provided clarification on the closure of 9,171 churches and mosques across the country, citing non-compliance with legal and governance requirements.
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda - The Rwanda Governance Board (RGB) has provided clarification on the closure of 9,171 churches and mosques across the country, citing non-compliance with legal and governance requirements. Some of the institutions may be reopened in the future depending on whether they meet the standards set by RGB, the agency said during a presentation in Parliament on 19 November 2025.

Dr. Doris Uwiceza Picard, Director General of RGB, explained that the closures followed special inspections of faith-based organizations during the 2024/2025 fiscal year. These inspections revealed issues including heretical teachings, financial mismanagement, lack of transparency, conflicts over leadership, and buildings not complying with legal provisions.

Of the 13,770 churches and mosques inspected, 9,171 were closed, while 21 organizations had their legal status revoked. RGB has engaged in discussions with religious leaders to improve compliance, governance, and building standards to prevent such issues in the future.

The Parliament raised concerns over the strict registration requirements introduced in March 2025, which mandate that new religious organizations must submit 1,000 supporter signatures and pay a non-refundable Rwf 2 million registration fee. Deputy Ntezimana Jean Claude questioned whether such high requirements were practical, especially for smaller congregations.

Dr. Uwiceza Picard defended the regulations, stating they were designed based on identified problems within faith-based organizations. She emphasized that these measures are meant to protect the population from misleading teachings and unregulated activities, and that the rules were discussed with religious representatives before implementation.

RGB also reported that in 2024/2025, it received 49 applications for legal status, of which only three were granted. Additionally, 23 organizations requested certificates of conformity with the law, and only one was approved.

Dr. Uwiceza Picard concluded that the closures and regulations are part of RGB’s ongoing mission to ensure transparency, accountability, and proper governance within Rwanda’s religious sector, while maintaining respect for freedom of worship.

title: Nigeria: Rwandan Student Film Wins International Award
excerpt: Kigali/Nigeria, November 22, 2025 - A group of Rwandan students won an international award at the International Students’ Film Festival in Nigeria for their film ‘Forgotten Frame’, which tells the story of a disabled…
title_en: Nigeria: Rwandan Student Film Wins International Award
excerpt_en: Kigali/Nigeria, November 22, 2025 - A group of Rwandan students won an international award at the International Students’ Film Festival in Nigeria for their film ‘Forgotten Frame’, which tells the story of a disabled…
body_en:
Kigali/Nigeria, November 22, 2025 - A group of Rwandan students won an international award at the International Students’ Film Festival in Nigeria for their film ‘Forgotten Frame’, which tells the story of a disabled child rejected by his father who later becomes famous.

The film brought together more than 40 students from Mount Kigali University and was directed by their teacher, Apollo Dusabimana O’Keefe, Secretary General of the Rwanda Film Association, who accompanied them to the festival.

The story follows a child born with a disability, whose father rejects him, unaware of the child’s talent. Migambi Elite Alexis, who wrote the film, said the award inspired him to work harder, marking his first international project.

He said, “Winning an award at the African level is a joy and a strength. You represent the country, and bringing back an award shows that things are possible.”

Nsabimana Elissa, a student involved in the project, said she initially doubted the film would reach African recognition, but the guidance of their director with over 20 years of experience showed them that nothing is impossible.

During the screening in Nigeria, the jury members were moved to tears, impressed by the message of the film, Dusabimana explained.

He added, “We competed in the humanities category. Everyone cried. Our film stood out because of the message it conveyed.”

The festival featured about 250 films from different universities, and the Rwandan team faced strong competition. The film highlighted African life and experiences, which resonated with the jury.

Following the festival, the students secured a partnership with the Nigerian Filmmakers Association to bring Nigerian actors and trainers to Rwanda. Dusabimana said, “Next year, we hope to implement this training program to develop the film industry in Rwanda.”

The production and editing of the film took 10 months and cost between 6 million and 8.5 million Rwandan francs (Rwf).

title: Minister Nsengimana Emphasizes Duty of Inclusive Education for People with Disabilities
excerpt: Kigali, 27 November 2025 - The Minister of Education, Joseph Nsengimana, has underscored that educating people with disabilities is not an act of pity but a national duty, stressing the importance of inclusive education…
title_en: Minister Nsengimana Emphasizes Duty of Inclusive Education for People with Disabilities
excerpt_en: Kigali, 27 November 2025 - The Minister of Education, Joseph Nsengimana, has underscored that educating people with disabilities is not an act of pity but a national duty, stressing the importance of inclusive education…
body_en:
Kigali, 27 November 2025 - The Minister of Education, Joseph Nsengimana, has underscored that educating people with disabilities is not an act of pity but a national duty, stressing the importance of inclusive education at all levels. He delivered the message during the launch of a two-day conference on inclusive education policy, which seeks to assess progress and identify areas needing reinforcement.

Minister Nsengimana highlighted that more than 5,000 schools across Rwanda now have at least one teacher trained to identify children with disabilities. This ensures that students receive tailored support to help them keep pace with their studies.

He further emphasized the introduction of assistive technology, noting that 73 centers have been equipped with devices that convert regular text into Braille, enabling visually impaired students to learn more effectively.

“Educating children with disabilities is not a matter of pity, but a responsibility, just like we teach all children,” Nsengimana said. “These children are the Rwanda of tomorrow. If we don’t educate them, we are not preparing the country for anything. It is important that we educate all children because it is the government’s program.”

Ndayisaba Emmanuel, Executive Secretary of the National Council for Persons with Disabilities, expressed gratitude for the country’s efforts in education, employment, sports, healthcare, and accessibility tools such as prosthetics, braces, and insurance coverage.

Nyirahabinshuti Beatha, a blind teacher at GS Gisozi I, shared her personal journey, highlighting that disability does not limit potential. “I competed for a teaching position like everyone else and was selected based on my abilities, not out of compassion. I currently teach English to fourth-year primary students, with only minor assistance for writing on the blackboard,” she said. She called for improved infrastructure in schools to make workplaces more accessible for people with disabilities.

Abizeyimana Justin, a specialist in teaching children with disabilities at Umubano Academy, pointed out the challenges students face in standardized exams. He argued that children with disabilities require adapted testing methods and access to appropriate learning materials to perform effectively.

Simununa Benitha, a deaf primary school student, highlighted communication barriers in classrooms where teachers and peers often do not know sign language. She stressed the need to expand sign language instruction for both teachers and students to enhance learning and inclusion.

The conference represents Rwanda’s commitment to inclusive education, aiming to ensure that students with disabilities are not left behind. By improving teaching methods, infrastructure, and assistive tools, the country seeks to empower all children to reach their full potential and actively contribute to national development.

title: Rwanda FDA Inspector Arrested Over Alleged Corruption and Bribery Scheme
excerpt: The Rwanda Investigation Bureau (RIB) has arrested an inspector from the Rwanda Food and Drug Authority (Rwanda FDA) along with a brewery owner on suspicion of corruption, according to a statement released on November…
title_en: Rwanda FDA Inspector Arrested Over Alleged Corruption and Bribery Scheme
excerpt_en: The Rwanda Investigation Bureau (RIB) has arrested an inspector from the Rwanda Food and Drug Authority (Rwanda FDA) along with a brewery owner on suspicion of corruption, according to a statement released on November…
body_en:
The Rwanda Investigation Bureau (RIB) has arrested an inspector from the Rwanda Food and Drug Authority (Rwanda FDA) along with a brewery owner on suspicion of corruption, according to a statement released on November 17, 2025.

The Rwanda FDA employee is accused of soliciting and receiving bribes from the owner of DUSANGIRE PRODUCTION Ltd, a brewery based in Bugesera District. According to RIB, the bribes were allegedly paid in exchange for exemption from routine inspections conducted by the regulatory authority. The inspector is also under investigation for breach of professional secrecy.

The brewery owner, a woman whose name has not been released, was also arrested in connection with the case.

RIB confirmed that both suspects are being held at its stations in Nyarugenge and Nyamata, and their case files have been submitted to the National Public Prosecution Authority for further action.

“RIB warns those who produce substandard products that they should stop doing so because it is against the law,” the statement emphasized. The agency also cautioned public officials against abusing their authority for personal gain, stressing that such acts are criminal and will not be tolerated.

The arrests come amid a broader crackdown on substandard production in recent days. Four factories have recently been shut down, including Joyland Company Ltd - producer of the Salama juice - and NI&P Ltd in Nyarugenge, both cited for manufacturing products that failed to meet required standards.

title: Trial of Manzi Sezisoni Postponed Again by Gasabo High Court
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda - The Gasabo High Court has once again postponed the trial of Manzi Sezisoni Davis, who faces multiple charges, including obtaining property through fraud, money laundering, and illegal currency trading.
title_en: Trial of Manzi Sezisoni Postponed Again by Gasabo High Court
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda - The Gasabo High Court has once again postponed the trial of Manzi Sezisoni Davis, who faces multiple charges, including obtaining property through fraud, money laundering, and illegal currency trading.
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda - The Gasabo High Court has once again postponed the trial of Manzi Sezisoni Davis, who faces multiple charges, including obtaining property through fraud, money laundering, and illegal currency trading.

The case involves allegations that Manzi defrauded citizens of over $10 million through a company called Billion Traders, promising investors significant profits. While the accused claims to have repaid 7 billion Rwandan francs, the Prosecution says no evidence has been provided to support this claim.

Authorities had previously requested a 15-year prison sentence for Manzi Davis and his wife, Akaliza, along with a $52 million fine. The case was reopened to allow plaintiffs to present their claims.

During the hearing on September 29, 2025, more than 100 plaintiffs stated that the agreements they made with Manzi Sezisoni should serve as conclusive evidence of his crimes. Manzi, however, argued that the agreements were unfulfilled and therefore should not constitute a crime. He asked the court to release him so that he could pursue funds frozen in an account he claims were meant to repay his creditors.

Manzi also stated that while he was abroad, it would have been easier to recover more than $2.5 million seized by the ICE Market Agency, following prosecution by judicial authorities.

The hearing, originally scheduled for October 18, 2025, has now been postponed to December 5, 2025.

Manzi Sezisoni has been detained at Nyarugenge Prison in Mageragere since August 29, 2024, following an order by the Gasabo Primary Court.

title: Huye: 25-Year-Old Found Hanging from a Tree, Police Investigate
excerpt: Huye, Rwanda - Authorities are investigating the death of a 25-year-old man found hanging from a tree in Mpare Cell, Tumba Sector, Huye District.
title_en: Huye: 25-Year-Old Found Hanging from a Tree, Police Investigate
excerpt_en: Huye, Rwanda - Authorities are investigating the death of a 25-year-old man found hanging from a tree in Mpare Cell, Tumba Sector, Huye District.
body_en:
Huye, Rwanda - Authorities are investigating the death of a 25-year-old man found hanging from a tree in Mpare Cell, Tumba Sector, Huye District. The incident was discovered on the morning of November 19, 2025, around 6:00 a.m., as residents began their daily routines.

According to neighbors, the young man, who sold samosas in Dansingi Center, had no known conflicts with family or community members. This has led locals to suspect foul play rather than suicide. One resident said, “Here in Mpare, there is a local beer called dundubwonko; many who drink it lose their humanity. Killing someone is not a crime to them. It is possible that he was killed and then hanged.”

Southern Province Police Spokesperson, CIP Kamanzi Hassan, confirmed that the authorities responded promptly after receiving reports from residents and local leaders. The body was taken to Butare University Hospital (CHUB) for an autopsy.

“Initial information indicates he had no conflict with his family. We are waiting for the investigation to determine the cause of death,” CIP Kamanzi stated. He expressed condolences to the victim’s family and assured them that all necessary steps would be taken to ensure justice through a thorough investigation.

Authorities have appealed to the public to share any information that could assist in clarifying the circumstances surrounding the death and expedite the investigation.

title: Rwanda Trains Justice Sector Workers on Human Rights and Prisoner Protection
excerpt: Nyanza, Rwanda - November 2025. The National Human Rights Commission (NCHR) has launched a new phase of training aimed at strengthening the protection of human rights, particularly for individuals in the early stages of…
title_en: Rwanda Trains Justice Sector Workers on Human Rights and Prisoner Protection
excerpt_en: Nyanza, Rwanda - November 2025. The National Human Rights Commission (NCHR) has launched a new phase of training aimed at strengthening the protection of human rights, particularly for individuals in the early stages of…
body_en:
Nyanza, Rwanda - November 2025. The National Human Rights Commission (NCHR) has launched a new phase of training aimed at strengthening the protection of human rights, particularly for individuals in the early stages of arrest and detention. The three-day workshop, held from 19-21 November 2025 at the Institute of Legal Practice and Development (ILPD) in Nyanza, follows an earlier session organized in Musanze on 11-14 November.

Bringing together 77 justice sector professionals, the training convened leaders from the Rwanda Investigation Bureau (RIB), Police, Prosecution, Judiciary, village authorities, lawyers, and officials from the Ministry of Justice (MINIJUST). Participants from the Northern and Western Provinces had attended the earlier Musanze session.

Dr. Yves Sezirahiga, ILPD’s Deputy Director for Academic Affairs and Research, praised the initiative for uniting institutions that often work separately.

“It is rare anywhere in the world to have RIB, Police, Prosecution, Judiciary, and Lawyers sit together to discuss human rights,” he said. “We thank the NCHR for bringing us together.”

He emphasized the need for a shared understanding of proper conduct during arrests and detentions, noting that a recent study revealed serious prison overcrowding, which can unintentionally lead to violations of prisoner rights. Rwanda currently ranks third globally for prison population density, he said.

Dr. Sezirahiga urged officers and prosecutors to uphold minimum standards of dignity when handling detainees and reminded them that no suspect should be questioned without access to a lawyer. He also called on judges to use alternative penalties where possible to help reduce overcrowding.

NCHR Chairperson Umurungi Providence said the training fosters collective learning across the justice system.

“We want participants to share experiences and good practices,” she said. “This will help raise standards and reinforce a culture of respecting human rights, especially in preventing harassment, abuse, and other inhumane acts.”

She acknowledged concerns about negligence among some justice sector staff and urged all actors to fulfill their responsibilities, particularly in protecting the rights of detainees.

Participants expressed optimism that the training would improve their daily work, noting that it provided concrete examples of effective practices used by colleagues across the sector.

The NCHR concluded by encouraging all institutions and communities to remain vigilant in preventing human rights violations and promoting accountability throughout the justice chain.

title: Rwanda: Minister Nsanzimana Highlights Health Benefits of Vehicle Emissions Testing
excerpt: The Minister of Health, Dr. Sabin Nsanzimana, has underscored the significant health benefits expected from Rwanda’s new vehicle emissions testing program, noting that it will help reduce the high prevalence of…
title_en: Rwanda: Minister Nsanzimana Highlights Health Benefits of Vehicle Emissions Testing
excerpt_en: The Minister of Health, Dr. Sabin Nsanzimana, has underscored the significant health benefits expected from Rwanda’s new vehicle emissions testing program, noting that it will help reduce the high prevalence of…
body_en:
The Minister of Health, Dr. Sabin Nsanzimana, has underscored the significant health benefits expected from Rwanda’s new vehicle emissions testing program, noting that it will help reduce the high prevalence of respiratory illnesses nationwide. He delivered the message on Saturday, November 22, 2025, after his own vehicle underwent testing and was confirmed compliant with national standards.

The inspection took place at the new Police Vehicle Inspection Center in Ndera, Kigali, where State Minister for Education, Claudette Irere, was also among those who participated in the emissions test.

Both officials urged the public to recognize the importance of emissions control in improving air quality and protecting public health.

Dr. Nsanzimana noted that exhaust fumes affect many people who do not drive or own vehicles, stressing the collective responsibility to maintain cleaner air.

“While exercising, a car may pass by and release fumes directly into your face,” he explained. “This is why I came to ensure that the vehicle I drive does not emit harmful smoke into the air and onto the people it passes.”

He emphasized that vehicle exhaust contains more harmful pollutants than other sources of air pollution, including dangerous gases like carbon monoxide (CO)-not just the CO₂ humans naturally exhale.

“Breathing in toxic gases from poorly maintained vehicles exposes people to serious respiratory diseases, including lung cancer,” he said. “During the rainy season, respiratory illnesses already increase due to flu viruses, and polluted air only makes the situation worse.”

Dr. Nsanzimana expressed confidence that widespread adoption of emissions testing will reduce respiratory diseases in a manner similar to how nationwide speed radars have helped reduce traffic accidents.

“Those speed radars have caught me several times, but they have reduced accidents and deaths. At first it may seem bothersome, but overall, the benefits are clear. We expect the same results for diseases caused by air pollution.”

State Minister Claudette Irere highlighted the importance of clean air for students, who travel daily along heavily polluted roads.

“Every day, children commute to school, and they are the first victims of polluted air,” she said. “We all have a role to play. Clean air keeps children healthy and helps them learn better.”

Irere added that emissions testing remains new to many Rwandans, prompting the Ministry of Education to explore integrating air quality education into the curriculum.

Vehicle emissions testing is now offered nationwide as an additional service to regular mechanical inspections, mainly in police inspection centers.

According to the Ministry of Environment, which launched the emissions control campaign on August 1, 2025, a total of 9,118 vehicles have been tested across the country. Among them, 77.4% passed, while 22.6% failed and were required to undergo repairs to meet greenhouse gas emissions standards.

The Rwanda Environment Management Authority (REMA) emphasized that Rwanda’s air contains PM2.5 fine particles, largely emitted by vehicles. These particles are closely monitored to assess whether a vehicle presents a health risk to the population.

title: Rubavu Leaders Urge Residents to Mobilize Men in DRC Forests to Return to Rwanda
excerpt: Rubavu, Rwanda - Leaders from various sectors in Rubavu District have called on local residents to actively support efforts to bring back Rwandan men who remain in the forests of the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
title_en: Rubavu Leaders Urge Residents to Mobilize Men in DRC Forests to Return to Rwanda
excerpt_en: Rubavu, Rwanda - Leaders from various sectors in Rubavu District have called on local residents to actively support efforts to bring back Rwandan men who remain in the forests of the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
body_en:
Rubavu, Rwanda - Leaders from various sectors in Rubavu District have called on local residents to actively support efforts to bring back Rwandan men who remain in the forests of the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The campaign, aimed at encouraging FDLR fighters to return home, has been ongoing since early 2025 with the support of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

During a campaign event on November 18, 2025, Rubavu District Mayor Mulindwa Prosper highlighted that most of the individuals voluntarily returning from the DRC are women and children, while men, particularly the youth, remain hesitant.

“Among those who voluntarily returned from the DRC, the majority are women and children, which shows that men, especially the youth, are still reluctant to return and have no reason to stay in the DRC,” the Mayor said.

He emphasized that local leaders, businesspeople, religious leaders, security forces, former FDLR members, and the general population must work together to encourage reluctant men to come back. “We should find strategies together for them to return to their country because the longer they stay there, the worse it will be for them. Rwanda grants them all their rights and the necessary documents, and welcomes everyone who returns on the journey to rebuild the country,” Mulindwa added.

Gen Maj (Rtd) Jacques Nziza, Vice President of the National Commission for the Rehabilitation of Former Soldiers (RDRC), echoed the Mayor’s sentiments, stressing that youth in the DRC forests should not follow the elders of the FDLR who refuse to return.

“Rwandans have been exiled from their homeland by the evil campaign of the FDLR. There is nothing more important than calling on them to return home. Leaders, religious leaders, take the lead in bringing back our children… We want to work with you to bring back our men. Some are afraid to return home because of shame and the years they have spent there. We will bring them all back,” Nziza said.

The Rwanda-DRC peace agreement, signed on June 27, 2025, provides for the disarmament and repatriation of FDLR fighters, alongside efforts to return Rwandan and Congolese refugees. Despite a campaign launched by the DRC military on October 10, tangible results have been limited, with only 12 former combatants returning with UN peacekeeping assistance.

Some FDLR fighters surrendered following the takeover of Goma by the AFC/M23 coalition in late January. Those who returned were welcomed at the RDRC facility in Mutobo, Musanze District, where they received vocational training and civic education to facilitate reintegration into Rwandan society.

On October 30, 2025, the RDRC repatriated 143 Rwandans, including former armed group members and their families, after providing training programs and support services to help them rebuild their lives.

title: Rwanda Welcomes Over 500 Returnees from the DRC
excerpt: Rubavu, Rwanda - 20 November 2025 - Rwanda has welcomed 511 Rwandans from 153 families who had been held hostage by the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
title_en: Rwanda Welcomes Over 500 Returnees from the DRC
excerpt_en: Rubavu, Rwanda - 20 November 2025 - Rwanda has welcomed 511 Rwandans from 153 families who had been held hostage by the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
body_en:
Rubavu, Rwanda - 20 November 2025 - Rwanda has welcomed 511 Rwandans from 153 families who had been held hostage by the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The returnees crossed through the La Corniche border, the main entry point connecting Rwanda and the DRC, and were received with vehicles to transport them to the Nyarushishi Center in Rusizi District for temporary accommodation and orientation.

The group included 127 women, 32 men, and 352 children, who had previously been living in the Goma temporary camp after fleeing various areas in eastern DRC. These Rwandans represent survivors who were forcibly displaced following the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.

Deputy Mayor of Rubavu District in charge of Economic Development, Nzabonimpa Deogratias, welcomed the returnees and emphasized the support programs in place to reintegrate them into society.

“They will be provided with basic necessities that will help them earn a living and serve the country. This support is part of Rwanda’s comprehensive strategy to integrate returnees into their communities. They will also be assisted to participate in community projects so they can provide for their families,” Nzabonimpa said.

He further highlighted that the increasing number of returnees reflects the effectiveness of ongoing mobilization campaigns, noting that both family members and peers of those still in the DRC are actively encouraging voluntary return.

Each returnee will receive financial support and essential supplies to facilitate their reintegration:

Adults (over 18 years old): $188 each

Children (under 18 years old): $113 each

Food assistance: valued at 45,000 Rwf per person

The Rwandan government, in coordination with local authorities and humanitarian agencies, continues to implement programs that ensure the safe and dignified return of Rwandans from the DRC, offering them opportunities to rebuild their lives and contribute to the country’s development.

title: AFC/M23 Commits to Dismantling Armed Groups in the DRC
excerpt: Kinshasa, DRC - 20 November 2025 - The AFC/M23 coalition, currently operating in eastern DRC, has announced its commitment to participating in the dismantling of armed groups across the country.
title_en: AFC/M23 Commits to Dismantling Armed Groups in the DRC
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, DRC - 20 November 2025 - The AFC/M23 coalition, currently operating in eastern DRC, has announced its commitment to participating in the dismantling of armed groups across the country.
body_en:
Kinshasa, DRC - 20 November 2025 - The AFC/M23 coalition, currently operating in eastern DRC, has announced its commitment to participating in the dismantling of armed groups across the country. This declaration was made during a press conference held by the coalition’s Permanent Secretary, Benjamin Mbonimpa.

Mbonimpa emphasized that the coalition’s engagement aligns with the basic principles agreed upon with the DRC government five days ago in Doha, Qatar, which outline cooperation between the government and the coalition to restore governance and security in the country.

“We will participate in dismantling armed groups operating in the DRC. We are not among those who will lay down our arms, but we will join the national army being established, as our army is moral and professional,” Mbonimpa stated.

The Doha agreement also includes provisions for collaboration in disbanding foreign armed groups active in DRC territory.

Mbonimpa further explained that the restoration of state authority and public services is a priority, given the limited capacity of the government to fully govern some regions.

“The fundamental principles are not just for one area; they apply to all of Congo. The country is not fully governed, and this will require changes in leadership throughout,” he said.

The coalition described the agreement as the first step in a broader process, with subsequent discussions expected to provide further clarity on the implementation of these commitments.

title: South Kivu: Renewed Violence as FDLR and CNRD Intensify Attacks on Civilians
excerpt: The FDLR and CNRD, two armed groups opposed to the Rwandan government, are reported to have intensified attacks on civilians in South Kivu, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, according to several regional sources.
title_en: South Kivu: Renewed Violence as FDLR and CNRD Intensify Attacks on Civilians
excerpt_en: The FDLR and CNRD, two armed groups opposed to the Rwandan government, are reported to have intensified attacks on civilians in South Kivu, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, according to several regional sources.
body_en:
The FDLR and CNRD, two armed groups opposed to the Rwandan government, are reported to have intensified attacks on civilians in South Kivu, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, according to several regional sources.

In a statement released by Lawrence Kanyuka, spokesperson for the AFC/M23 coalition currently fighting the Congolese army, the groups-alongside the FARDC, the Burundian army, the Wazalendo militias, and the Cancuro-have launched military operations since November 19, 2025, in several densely populated areas of the province.

On the evening of November 21, Sukhoi fighter jets conducted airstrikes on Mikenke and Rwitsankuku, near the Banyamulenge refugee camp, around 7:00 p.m. Kanyuka accused the coalition forces of using warplanes, drones, and long-range artillery, resulting in civilian casualties and widespread displacement.

The AFC/M23 leadership warned that the escalation represents a serious setback to the progress made on November 15, when the movement and the DRC government signed the Basic Principles, a framework intended to pave the way toward lasting peace.

Despite the ongoing clashes, the alliance stated that it would continue to “protect civilians and defend them” as confrontations escalate across South Kivu.

title: DRC Government and AFC/M23 Trade Accusations Over Ceasefire Violations
excerpt: The Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 alliance are accusing each other of violating the ceasefire in several areas of North Kivu and South Kivu, escalating tensions in the…
title_en: DRC Government and AFC/M23 Trade Accusations Over Ceasefire Violations
excerpt_en: The Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 alliance are accusing each other of violating the ceasefire in several areas of North Kivu and South Kivu, escalating tensions in the…
body_en:
The Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 alliance are accusing each other of violating the ceasefire in several areas of North Kivu and South Kivu, escalating tensions in the conflict-hit eastern region.

On November 22, 2025, DRC military spokesman Gen. Maj. Sylvain Ekenge told reporters that the AFC/M23 continues to launch attacks despite the ceasefire agreement. He called on the Government of Qatar and the United States-both guarantors of the deal-to take action against the rebel coalition.

“Every day, the AFC/M23 alliance continues to carry out attacks on our positions, violating the ceasefire,” said Gen. Maj. Ekenge.

His statement came after a DRC Sukhoi fighter jet conducted airstrikes on November 21 in Mikenke and Rwitsankuku in South Kivu, and in Kibanda, located in Masisi territory in North Kivu.

By the morning of November 22, the FARDC, supported by Wazalendo militia groups, had resumed heavy fighting with AFC/M23 fighters in Kibanda and Katoi, both in Masisi.

In response, AFC/M23 Permanent Secretary Benjamin Mbonimpa rejected the allegations, insisting that government forces-not the alliance-were responsible for breaking the truce.

“AFC/M23 is not the one violating the ceasefire, nor is it to blame for the consequences that follow,” he said, adding that the FARDC claims “it has a duty to restore calm by all means,” while the alliance is equally entitled to “defend itself.”

The renewed clashes violate the ceasefire agreement signed by both parties with the mediation of the State of Qatar. The deal included the creation of a monitoring mechanism, expected to include representatives from the DRC, AFC/M23, Qatar, the United States, and the African Union (AU). However, this body has not yet begun its work, contributing to growing uncertainty around the agreement's implementation.

title: AFC/M23 Expands Strongholds in Walikale, North Kivu
excerpt: Walikale, North Kivu, November 23, 2025 - The AFC/M23 coalition, fighting the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government, continues to expand its strongholds in the Walikale territory, an area where the opposition is…
title_en: AFC/M23 Expands Strongholds in Walikale, North Kivu
excerpt_en: Walikale, North Kivu, November 23, 2025 - The AFC/M23 coalition, fighting the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government, continues to expand its strongholds in the Walikale territory, an area where the opposition is…
body_en:
Walikale, North Kivu, November 23, 2025 - The AFC/M23 coalition, fighting the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government, continues to expand its strongholds in the Walikale territory, an area where the opposition is already dominant.

Earlier in 2025, AFC/M23 had established strongholds in the region, but the Doha peace talks forced them to retreat, leaving Walikale town in April to negotiate with the DRC government.

The coalition has been engaged in ongoing clashes with DRC forces, allied with the Wazalendo, in North Kivu. On November 22, fighting erupted in Masisi territory, resulting in AFC/M23 capturing the centers of Mahanga and Kibanda in Osso Byanyungu Gurupoma.

On November 23, AFC/M23 launched a major attack on RDC and Wazalendo positions in Buhimba center, Waloa Yungu commune, Walikale territory. As seen in previous operations in Masisi, RDC and Wazalendo forces withdrew, heading to Kailenge and Luhando, where they reportedly burned down their bases.

The capture of Buhimba center enabled AFC/M23 fighters to seize other key locations in Walikale, including Kimua and Ntoto.

Earlier, on November 21, AFC/M23 had captured Kaliki center, also in Waloa Yungu, Walikale, reportedly possessing advanced military equipment, including rifles.

title: Uvira: Four Dead, Many Injured in FARDC-Wazalendo Clashes
excerpt: Uvira, South Kivu, November 23, 2025 - The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) army, FARDC, reported that four people were killed and 14 others injured in clashes with Wazalendo fighters in the town of Uvira, South Kivu…
title_en: Uvira: Four Dead, Many Injured in FARDC-Wazalendo Clashes
excerpt_en: Uvira, South Kivu, November 23, 2025 - The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) army, FARDC, reported that four people were killed and 14 others injured in clashes with Wazalendo fighters in the town of Uvira, South Kivu…
body_en:
Uvira, South Kivu, November 23, 2025 - The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) army, FARDC, reported that four people were killed and 14 others injured in clashes with Wazalendo fighters in the town of Uvira, South Kivu province.

The incident occurred when the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) was distributing food at the Munanira school, near the Uvira Cathedral. Armed Wazalendo fighters attacked and attempted to seize the supplies by force.

DRC soldiers, including members of the Panthers and the civilian rescue battalion, responded, but the Wazalendo refused to comply, sparking heavy fighting involving small and heavy arms fire.

The clashes forced aid workers and football fans to seek refuge at a nearby church, where many others were celebrating Catholic Youth Day.

Lt Mbuyi Kalonji Reagan, spokesman for the DRC military in South Kivu, confirmed that calm had returned, but reported four deaths, including a government soldier, two Wazalendo, and one civilian.

He also confirmed 14 injuries, including two soldiers, nine civilians, and three Wazalendo fighters. Soldiers were treated at a military hospital, while civilians received care at the Uvira General Hospital.

Lt Mbuyi added that the attackers were not genuine Wazalendo, but were allegedly being used by enemies to create chaos in government-controlled areas and disrupt local security.

title: Mwenga: AFC/M23 Captures Two Areas, FARDC Repels Them
excerpt: Mwenga, South Kivu, November 24, 2025 - The AFC/M23 coalition, fighting the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government, captured the Kitwabaluzi and Kilungutwe areas in Mwenga territory, forcing government troops to…
title_en: Mwenga: AFC/M23 Captures Two Areas, FARDC Repels Them
excerpt_en: Mwenga, South Kivu, November 24, 2025 - The AFC/M23 coalition, fighting the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government, captured the Kitwabaluzi and Kilungutwe areas in Mwenga territory, forcing government troops to…
body_en:
Mwenga, South Kivu, November 24, 2025 - The AFC/M23 coalition, fighting the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government, captured the Kitwabaluzi and Kilungutwe areas in Mwenga territory, forcing government troops to flee on foot. The clashes began in the morning of November 24 and intensified throughout the day.

After seizing these areas at 5:00 p.m., DRC forces and their allies, the Wazalendo, retreated toward Cidasa center in Luindi sheriff. Local residents reported that fleeing troops looted shops and property, including goats and motorcycles.

The fighting between AFC/M23 and DRC-Wazalendo forces continues across several parts of North Kivu and South Kivu provinces. On November 23, AFC/M23 had captured Buhimba center in the Gurupoma of Waloa Yungu, Walikale territory, but withdrew on November 24 after a counterattack by DRC and Wazalendo forces, returning to Kasopo.

AFC/M23 spokesman Lawrence Kanyuka announced that DRC government forces are conducting attacks in densely populated areas, using Sukhoi-25 aircraft, combat drones, and long-range artillery.

He said, “Sukhoi-25 fighter jets are returning frequently, accompanied by combat drones and long-range artillery. These attacks by Kinshasa put civilians in grave danger.”

On November 23, AFC/M23 stated it would not tolerate attacks on its positions and civilians, asserting its right to defend itself and protect those at risk.

title: Israeli Veterans Visit Rwanda, Excited for First Trip to Africa
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda - November 25, 2025 - A group of 14 Israeli veterans, rehabilitated after being injured in combat, visited Rwanda, marking their first return to the African continent.
title_en: Israeli Veterans Visit Rwanda, Excited for First Trip to Africa
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda - November 25, 2025 - A group of 14 Israeli veterans, rehabilitated after being injured in combat, visited Rwanda, marking their first return to the African continent.
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda - November 25, 2025 - A group of 14 Israeli veterans, rehabilitated after being injured in combat, visited Rwanda, marking their first return to the African continent. The delegation was warmly received by the Israeli Ambassador to Rwanda, Einat Weiss.

Among the visitors, Moti Harari, a mostly disabled soldier from the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF), expressed excitement about the trip. “We are happy to be back in Rwanda and look forward to learning a lot during our week-long stay,” he said.

The veterans are accommodated at the Beit Halochem facility, a center supporting wounded soldiers through cultural, recreational, and sports activities. While private, the Israeli government supports five such centers to aid in the rehabilitation of former soldiers.

Beit Halochem’s Sports Director, Miki Uzai, highlighted the significance of the visit. “Arriving in Rwanda is an exciting experience because it is our first time in Africa. We have visited Paris, London, and Vancouver, but this is special. We are grateful to the Embassy, the Government of Israel, and the Government of Rwanda,” he said.

Uzai noted Rwanda’s development in coffee and tea exports and recognized the country as one of the leading nations on the African continent. “Compared to the 54 African countries, Rwanda ranks among the best,” he added.

During their stay, the veterans are expected to visit the Kigali Genocide Memorial to honor victims of the Genocide against the Tutsi and learn about Rwanda’s history and recovery. They will also experience gorilla trekking, and participate in friendly sports games, including Wheelchair Basketball.

This visit is seen as an opportunity to strengthen cultural understanding, celebrate resilience, and promote recreational rehabilitation for the veterans.

title: Rwanda Receives 15 FDLR Fighters and Civilians Repatriated From DRC
excerpt: Kigali, November 25, 2025 - Rwanda has received 15 ex-combatants of the FDLR and seven civilians associated with armed groups, repatriated from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) by personnel from the United Nations…
title_en: Rwanda Receives 15 FDLR Fighters and Civilians Repatriated From DRC
excerpt_en: Kigali, November 25, 2025 - Rwanda has received 15 ex-combatants of the FDLR and seven civilians associated with armed groups, repatriated from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) by personnel from the United Nations…
body_en:
Kigali, November 25, 2025 - Rwanda has received 15 ex-combatants of the FDLR and seven civilians associated with armed groups, repatriated from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) by personnel from the United Nations peacekeeping mission, MONUSCO. The group, which arrived on Tuesday, includes five children, according to officials.

The Chairperson of the National Commission for the Demobilization and Rehabilitation of Ex-Combatants (RDRC), Valerie Nyirahabineza, confirmed the development, noting that the total number of arrivals was 22 people.

“Today we received 22 forest residents, including 15 ex-combatants, seven civilians, and five children,” she told.

Nyirahabineza explained that once these former fighters arrive in Rwanda, they are immediately transferred to the Mutobo Demobilization and Reintegration Centre for a three- to four-month training program aimed at preparing them for reintegration into civilian life.

“When they come voluntarily, they receive training before being discharged and reunited with their families. We work with various institutions to assess them and ensure that their behavior has changed,” she said.

The training at Mutobo is designed to help ex-combatants abandon the negative ideology they were exposed to in the forests of eastern DRC, especially those from factions of the FDLR.

Upon arrival, the returnees also receive medical treatment, including support for trauma recovery, as many suffer psychological effects after years in armed groups.

“In addition to training, they receive assistance such as health care, shelter, food, clothing, and support tailored to women, children, the elderly, and persons with disabilities,” Nyirahabineza added.

She also urged former combatants who have already reintegrated into their communities to help encourage others still in the forests to demobilize and return home, stressing that Rwanda is ready to receive them.

According to RDRC figures, between January and October 2025, MONUSCO repatriated 54 Rwandan fighters, mostly from the FDLR, along with 44 family members.

Since 2001, the RDRC has processed 12,602 former members of Rwandan armed groups operating in eastern DRC, received in 75 batches following their demobilization.

title: Seven Killed in Fresh Clashes Between Wazalendo and FARDC in Uvira
excerpt: UVIRA, South Kivu - Two days of violent clashes between Wazalendo militias and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have left 11 people dead, including combatants from both sides and civilians.
title_en: Seven Killed in Fresh Clashes Between Wazalendo and FARDC in Uvira
excerpt_en: UVIRA, South Kivu - Two days of violent clashes between Wazalendo militias and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have left 11 people dead, including combatants from both sides and civilians.
body_en:
UVIRA, South Kivu - Two days of violent clashes between Wazalendo militias and the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have left 11 people dead, including combatants from both sides and civilians. The confrontation erupted on November 23, 2025, after FARDC troops blocked Wazalendo fighters attempting to loot humanitarian aid from the World Food Programme (WFP) destined for vulnerable residents of Uvira.

According to Lt. Reagan Mbuyi Kalonji, spokesman for FARDC operations in South Kivu, the initial fighting left four people dead-a government soldier, two Wazalendo combatants, and one civilian-while 14 others were injured.

Updated casualty figures released on November 25 indicate that five of the injured later died at the Uvira hospital, raising the death toll.

Fighting resumed on November 24, paralyzing daily activities in the city, with residents forced to close businesses and shelter indoors. That day, two additional people were killed and two others wounded.

FARDC confirmed that the two days of clashes resulted in the deaths of three government soldiers, three Wazalendo fighters, and several civilians whose number has not been fully disclosed.

This is not the first confrontation between the two forces. In September 2025, heavy fighting also erupted in Uvira when Wazalendo combatants attempted to expel Brig Gen Olivier Gasita, accusing him of being Umunyamulenge and therefore unfit to command operations in the region.

The latest clashes underscore FARDC’s growing difficulty in controlling Wazalendo militias, raising concerns among government officials. The internal friction threatens to undermine efforts to conduct coordinated operations against AFC/M23 rebels in strategic zones, including Uvira, where unity between security forces is crucial.

title: South Kivu: Burundian Troops Clash with AFC/M23 in Kasika
excerpt: KASIKA, Mwenga Territory - Intense fighting erupted between Burundian troops and AFC/M23 rebels in the center of Kasika on November 26, 2025, following the withdrawal of DRC forces and Wazalendo militias from several…
title_en: South Kivu: Burundian Troops Clash with AFC/M23 in Kasika
excerpt_en: KASIKA, Mwenga Territory - Intense fighting erupted between Burundian troops and AFC/M23 rebels in the center of Kasika on November 26, 2025, following the withdrawal of DRC forces and Wazalendo militias from several…
body_en:
KASIKA, Mwenga Territory - Intense fighting erupted between Burundian troops and AFC/M23 rebels in the center of Kasika on November 26, 2025, following the withdrawal of DRC forces and Wazalendo militias from several strategic areas in South Kivu. The clashes mark a new escalation in a rapidly deteriorating security situation.

On November 25, FARDC and Wazalendo units retreated from Kasika, Kamituga, and the Mwenga town axis, leaving behind a trail of looted homes and shops.A resident of Kasika described scenes of devastation: “They ransacked the shops, took everything. The people of Kasika are crying. They destroyed pharmacies, shops, cars, everything. They entered every room and emptied them.”

In Kamituga, witnesses reported Burundian soldiers beating and disarming a suspected FARDC soldier caught looting commercial establishments, further highlighting the breakdown of discipline within local units.

The retreat of government forces came after the AFC/M23 advanced and captured key positions in Mwenga, including Kilungutwe, Kitwabaluzi, Kalama, and Chowe. Their progress sparked alarm within the DRC government over the possibility that Mwenga center itself could soon fall.

At dawn on November 26, recognizing FARDC’s absence and collapse of defenses, Burundian troops re-entered Kasika and engaged the AFC/M23 rebels, who had seized control of the area the previous day. Sources in Mwenga confirmed that no DRC soldiers participated in the fighting - a pattern seen in previous confrontations when FARDC units withdraw upon facing intense resistance.

The involvement of the Burundian army signals the seriousness of the threat, as the AFC/M23 pushes closer to its strongholds in the highlands surrounding Minembwe, spanning the territories of Uvira, Fizi, and Mwenga.

For several days, AFC/M23 commanders have warned that if FARDC continues operations against their strongholds or densely populated areas under their influence, they will “defend themselves and the civilians under attack.”

Analysts warn that if Burundian forces lose Kasika, the AFC/M23 could gain momentum to seize additional territory across South Kivu - mirroring their sweeping gains earlier in the year when they forced government and coalition forces out of North Kivu.

title: FARDC Sukhoi-25 Jets Strike AFC/M23 Positions in Masisi and Walikale
excerpt: NORTH KIVU - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) launched airstrikes against AFC/M23 positions in the territories of Walikale and Masisi on the morning of November 27, 2025, deploying…
title_en: FARDC Sukhoi-25 Jets Strike AFC/M23 Positions in Masisi and Walikale
excerpt_en: NORTH KIVU - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) launched airstrikes against AFC/M23 positions in the territories of Walikale and Masisi on the morning of November 27, 2025, deploying…
body_en:
NORTH KIVU - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) launched airstrikes against AFC/M23 positions in the territories of Walikale and Masisi on the morning of November 27, 2025, deploying Sukhoi-25 fighter jets in an effort to halt rebel advances.

According to military sources, the strikes targeted rebel-held zones in Kibati (Walikale) and Kasopo (Masisi). The bombings coincided with an ongoing Wazalendo offensive on AFC/M23 positions in Kibati, involving both heavy and light weaponry.

AFC/M23 fighters have controlled Kibati for eight months. Although Wazalendo briefly recaptured four positions there on October 11, 2025, they withdrew after only two days. Since then, repeated joint attempts by Wazalendo and FARDC - supported by fighter jets and drones - have failed to reclaim the area.

Parallel clashes continue in South Kivu, particularly in Mwenga and Shabunda, where AFC/M23, Wazalendo militias, FARDC, and Burundian troops have engaged in heavy fighting for several consecutive days.

On November 26, Burundian forces suffered a major setback in Kasika (Mwenga), facing fierce resistance from AFC/M23 fighters before eventually retreating.

In response, FARDC deployed a Sukhoi-25 to strike AFC/M23 positions in Kasika. However, the airstrike failed to dislodge the rebels, who maintain firm control over the area.

title: Rwanda Engages Defence Attachés on Regional Security and Military Cooperation
excerpt: The Ministry of Defence hosted a high-level meeting in Kigali on 27 November 2025, bringing together Defence Attachés accredited to Rwanda for an extensive briefing on the country’s security environment and regional dynamics.
title_en: Rwanda Engages Defence Attachés on Regional Security and Military Cooperation
excerpt_en: The Ministry of Defence hosted a high-level meeting in Kigali on 27 November 2025, bringing together Defence Attachés accredited to Rwanda for an extensive briefing on the country’s security environment and regional dynamics.
body_en:
The Ministry of Defence hosted a high-level meeting in Kigali on 27 November 2025, bringing together Defence Attachés accredited to Rwanda for an extensive briefing on the country’s security environment and regional dynamics. The discussions also highlighted the role of the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) in peacekeeping operations and international military cooperation.

The delegation was received by Brig Gen Patrick Karuretwa, the Director General for International Military Cooperation, who led the technical session.

Rwanda Reaffirms Commitment to Peace and Cooperation

Minister of Defence Juvenal Marizamunda thanked the Defence Attachés for their continued partnership in supporting efforts to maintain peace and stability.

He emphasized that Rwanda remains fully committed to working with treaty partners and international organizations to confront evolving security challenges.

Brig Gen Karuretwa delivered a comprehensive briefing on the national and regional security situation, stressing the importance of:

Joint efforts to promote peace at both regional and global levels

Following the presentations, participants held open discussions, assessing shared security concerns, regional hotspots, and opportunities to deepen bilateral and multilateral defence cooperation.

The engagement underscored the RDF’s commitment to military diplomacy, fostering stronger relationships with friendly nations and enhancing mutual understanding of security priorities.

The conference gathered Defence Attachés and representatives from 25 countries and international organizations, including:

United States, France, United Kingdom, Germany, Russia, China, Japan, Israel, Jordan, Turkey, Sweden, Poland, Angola, Ghana, Botswana, South Korea, Zimbabwe, Sudan, Kenya, Czech Republic, Tanzania, Namibia, as well as the European Union (EU) and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).

Brig Gen Karuretwa delivered a comprehensive briefing on the national and regional security situation, stressing the importance of:

Joint efforts to promote peace at both regional and global levels

Following the presentations, participants held open discussions, assessing shared security concerns, regional hotspots, and opportunities to deepen bilateral and multilateral defence cooperation.

The engagement underscored the RDF’s commitment to military diplomacy, fostering stronger relationships with friendly nations and enhancing mutual understanding of security priorities.

The conference gathered Defence Attachés and representatives from 25 countries and international organizations, including:

United States, France, United Kingdom, Germany, Russia, China, Japan, Israel, Jordan, Turkey, Sweden, Poland, Angola, Ghana, Botswana, South Korea, Zimbabwe, Sudan, Kenya, Czech Republic, Tanzania, Namibia, as well as the European Union (EU) and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).

title: FDLR Ex-Leader Reveals Group’s Ties to Minerals and DRC Military Support
excerpt: Kigali, November 28, 2025 - Lt Col Mpakaniye Emilien, alias Che Guevara Jacob, a former leader in the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), has confirmed the role of both the FDLR and the Congolese army…
title_en: FDLR Ex-Leader Reveals Group’s Ties to Minerals and DRC Military Support
excerpt_en: Kigali, November 28, 2025 - Lt Col Mpakaniye Emilien, alias Che Guevara Jacob, a former leader in the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), has confirmed the role of both the FDLR and the Congolese army…
body_en:
Kigali, November 28, 2025 - Lt Col Mpakaniye Emilien, alias Che Guevara Jacob, a former leader in the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), has confirmed the role of both the FDLR and the Congolese army in mineral exploitation and the ongoing conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). His testimony sheds light on the illicit networks that have sustained the group’s operations for years.

Addressing military advisors from several embassies visiting Rwanda, Mpakaniye explained that between 2008 and 2010, he oversaw the FDLR’s mineral trade operations. He said the group collaborated with Congolese civilians and soldiers to extract precious minerals from mines in Rubaya and Bisie in Walikale, South Kivu, which were then sold to finance weapons purchases.

“That’s how the FDLR survived,” Mpakaniye said. “Selling precious stones allowed us to buy weapons and sustain the war, and the proceeds were also used for basic livelihoods. This illegal trade became a powerful instrument in the FDLR’s conflict.”

Mpakaniye asserted that the FDLR’s continued existence depends on support from the DRC government. He claimed that the FARDC (DRC army) provides weapons and ammunition to the group, both for operations in eastern DRC and for attacks against Rwanda.

“If the DRC government did not work with the FDLR, the FDLR would cease to exist,” he said. “The FARDC says the FDLR is helping fight the enemy, but they are also providing resources to attack Rwanda.”

He stressed that this information is not based solely on his personal experience but is corroborated by multiple reports, including investigations by United Nations experts.

After voluntarily returning to Rwanda, Mpakaniye described a dramatic change in perspective. Upon arriving at the Mutobo rehabilitation camp, he realized that the FDLR’s justification for attacking Rwanda was based on false narratives.

“I thought the FDLR had a legitimate reason to fight Rwanda, but after returning home, I saw that the group lied to us. Rwanda welcomed us, gave us resources, and helped us start a new life,” he said.

The Mutobo camp provides training and support for former fighters, aiming to reintegrate them into civilian life and remove the violent ideology they were taught in the forests of eastern DRC.

As of June 2025, the FDLR reportedly consisted of 7,000 to 10,000 fighters, with top leaders including Lt Gen Byiringiro Victor and Pacifique Ntawungua (“Gen Omega”) still operating in the mineral-rich Walikale territory. This region is known for deposits of Gasegereti, Coltan, and Wolfram, which have long been a source of illicit funding for armed groups.

Mpakaniye’s testimony underscores the complex interplay between rebel groups, state actors, and the mineral economy in the eastern DRC, highlighting the challenges of regional security and the efforts Rwanda has undertaken to rehabilitate former combatants peacefully.

title: DRC: Burundian Soldiers Buried in Mass Graves in Kasika
excerpt: Kasika, Mwenga, November 29, 2025 - The AFC/M23 coalition reported that several Burundian soldiers who died during recent clashes in Kasika, Mwenga, and surrounding areas were buried in mass graves.
title_en: DRC: Burundian Soldiers Buried in Mass Graves in Kasika
excerpt_en: Kasika, Mwenga, November 29, 2025 - The AFC/M23 coalition reported that several Burundian soldiers who died during recent clashes in Kasika, Mwenga, and surrounding areas were buried in mass graves.
body_en:
Kasika, Mwenga, November 29, 2025 - The AFC/M23 coalition reported that several Burundian soldiers who died during recent clashes in Kasika, Mwenga, and surrounding areas were buried in mass graves. According to Lt Col Willy Ngoma, the coalition’s military spokesperson, the burials were conducted hastily by fellow soldiers amid ongoing fighting.

“It is shameful and sad to see Burundian soldiers who were injured in Kasika, Kirungutwe, Mwenga being taken to Walikale and then forcibly taken to Kisangani instead of being returned to their homes. They were killed for the interests of one person,” Lt Col Ngoma stated. He added that numerous Burundian soldiers’ bodies were buried in mass graves in Kasika prior to further clashes with local forces.

The announcement comes amid continued unrest in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where clashes involve government forces, FARDC, Wazalendo, and M23 fighters. On November 25, 2025, DRC and Wazalendo forces withdrew from Kasika, Kamituga, and Mwenga town, leaving behind looted shops and homes, according to local sources.

Earlier, on November 23, the AFC/M23 coalition had captured the Buhimba center in Group of Waloa Yungu, Walikale territory. However, the coalition withdrew the following day after an offensive by DRC and Wazalendo forces, returning to Kasopo.

The reports highlight the intensity of clashes in South Kivu, the complex regional involvement of Burundian troops, and the ongoing struggle between the DRC government and various armed groups over strategic territories.

The second half of November 2025 highlights a stark contrast between Rwanda’s internal trajectory of economic modernization and diplomatic expansion, and the volatile security crisis escalating on its western border.

1. Regional Instability and Security Dilemmas The security situation in the Great Lakes region remains the primary challenge. Despite ongoing mediation efforts in Doha and Washington, distrust persists between the DRC and Rwanda. The conflict in Eastern DRC has intensified, with the AFC/M23 coalition making significant territorial gains in North and South Kivu, drawing in Burundian troops and engaging FARDC and Wazalendo forces.

Diplomatic Stance: Rwanda has adopted a firm posture, with Foreign Minister Nduhungirehe rejecting recent ICGLR resolutions as "irrelevant" and President Kagame issuing strong warnings regarding the security of Goma.

Mineral Dispute: The President also strongly rebuked European nations, accusing them of historical and ongoing looting of DRC minerals while scapegoating Rwanda.

Repatriation: On a positive note, efforts to demobilize FDLR fighters have yielded results, with over 500 Rwandans, including former combatants, returning home from the DRC during this period.

2. Diplomatic Leadership and Global Influence Kigali cemented its status as a diplomatic hub by hosting high-level summits.

Francophonie: The hosting of the 46th OIF Ministerial Meeting underscored Rwanda's influence within the Francophone world, with a specific focus on women's role in development.

Pan-Africanism: The African Renaissance Retreat, led by President Kagame and Aliko Dangote, brought together global leaders to discuss self-driven African solutions.

New Partnerships: Diplomatic ties were strengthened through new ambassadorships in Singapore and Lithuania , and the opening of a Swiss Embassy in Kigali.

3. Economic Resilience and Infrastructure Despite regional trade disruptions caused by post-election unrest in Tanzania, Rwanda’s economy shows resilience.

Trade Growth: The UAE and DRC have emerged as the top export destinations, with total exports reaching Rwf 3,955.5 billion.

Development: Key infrastructure projects, such as the Rubengera-Nyange road, were completed , and significant investments were made in public health, including a new Rwf 30 billion laboratory for zoonotic diseases.

4. Governance and Social Regulation Internally, the government maintained strict regulatory oversight.

Accountability: The Rwanda Governance Board closed over 9,000 non-compliant places of worship to ensure safety and proper governance.

Anti-Corruption: A crackdown on corruption saw arrests within the FDA and brewery sectors , aligning with AU recognition of Rwanda’s strong anti-corruption standing.

In summary, while Rwanda continues to advance its "Vision 2050" through aggressive economic diversification and strategic diplomacy, the deteriorating war in the Eastern DRC and the associated geopolitical fallout pose a critical threat that dominated the national agenda in late November 2025.

title: Mali’s Council of Ministers Approves Treasury Reform and Key Diplomatic Appointments
excerpt: Bamako, October 29, 2025 - Mali’s Council of Ministers, chaired by Colonel Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition, convened Wednesday at Koulouba Palace to address public finance reforms, diplomatic postings, and…
title_en: Mali’s Council of Ministers Approves Treasury Reform and Key Diplomatic Appointments
excerpt_en: Bamako, October 29, 2025 - Mali’s Council of Ministers, chaired by Colonel Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition, convened Wednesday at Koulouba Palace to address public finance reforms, diplomatic postings, and…
body_en:
Bamako, October 29, 2025 - Mali’s Council of Ministers, chaired by Colonel Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition, convened Wednesday at Koulouba Palace to address public finance reforms, diplomatic postings, and updates from various ministries.

The Council approved a draft decree establishing the organizational framework for the regional and sub-regional services of the Directorate General of the Treasury and Public Accounting. Proposed by the Minister of Economy and Finance, the reform aims to enhance efficiency in financial oversight and public accounting operations over the next five years.

The Directorate, created in September 2024, oversees national policies on finance, accounting, monetary affairs, insurance, and microfinance regulation, playing a central role in Mali’s public finance management.

Several key appointments were ratified across ministries:

Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation

Inspectors of Diplomatic and Consular Services: Sory Lakamine Diakité and Allaye Bah.

Ministry of Handicrafts, Culture, Hotel Industry and Tourism

Director General of the National Center for Cinematography of Mali: Sidy Lamine Bagayoko

The Minister of Territorial Administration and Decentralization briefed the Council on the crisis at Bamako’s Les Lutins primary school, triggered by the non-renewal of its parents’ association. A provisional administrative committee has been established to restore normal operations.

The Minister of Labour, Public Service and Social Dialogue highlighted Mali’s participation in the 6th Conference of Ministers of Labour of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in Doha, which adopted resolutions promoting employment and social protection among member states.

The Minister of Youth and Sports announced the 2025 African Youth Day celebrations under the theme “Fighting Drugs Among Youth: Awareness and Prevention.” The program will include cultural, educational, and sporting activities aimed at raising awareness on drug abuse.

The Minister of Environment, Sanitation and Sustainable Development reported on Mali’s participation in two international forums:

The Madrid Ministerial Meeting on Water, Hygiene, and Sanitation, which emphasized integrated sector governance and sustainable financing.

The World Zero Waste Forum in Istanbul, where Mali reaffirmed its goal to reduce waste emissions by 31% by 2030 and agreed with Turkey on joint recycling and waste transformation projects.

The Minister of Health and Social Development noted a nationwide decline in dengue fever cases, while President Goïta urged continued vigilance and adherence to public health measures.

The Council concluded by reaffirming Mali’s commitment to fiscal discipline, effective governance, and international cooperation.

title: Gao Authorities Boost Administrative Capacity and Extend Support to Vulnerable Groups
excerpt: Gao, Mali - The Malian government has reinforced its commitment to improving public service delivery and supporting vulnerable populations through a dual initiative spearheaded by Major General Moussa Traoré, Governor…
title_en: Gao Authorities Boost Administrative Capacity and Extend Support to Vulnerable Groups
excerpt_en: Gao, Mali - The Malian government has reinforced its commitment to improving public service delivery and supporting vulnerable populations through a dual initiative spearheaded by Major General Moussa Traoré, Governor…
body_en:
Gao, Mali - The Malian government has reinforced its commitment to improving public service delivery and supporting vulnerable populations through a dual initiative spearheaded by Major General Moussa Traoré, Governor of the Gao Region.

During a ceremony in Gao, Governor Traoré handed over computer equipment and office furniture to prefects and sub-prefects across the region, a move aimed at enhancing administrative efficiency and bringing government services closer to local communities.

"The highest authorities are equipping all State representatives, especially those assigned to newly established administrative areas," Maj. Gen. Traoré said. "This marks the beginning of broader efforts to improve the working and living conditions of public service staff."

Receiving the materials, Médian Koné, Prefect of the Ouattagouna Circle, expressed gratitude on behalf of his peers and pledged responsible use of the equipment."We assure the Ministry of Territorial Administration and Decentralization that the equipment will be properly maintained and used to serve the population effectively," he said.

In a parallel initiative, the Governor distributed food aid to vulnerable individuals and community organizations as part of Mali’s National Month of Solidarity, observed each October.

Maj. Gen. Traoré emphasized that while the donations were modest, they symbolized the government’s enduring support for the people of Gao."The value of giving lies not in the quantity, but in the spirit behind it," he said, thanking the President of the Transition and the Food Security Commission for backing the initiative.

Officials noted that these measures align with broader national efforts to strengthen governance, foster social cohesion, and ensure that administrative services remain accessible to citizens.

title: Malians Urged to Show Resilience and Unity Amid National Crisis
excerpt: Bamako, Mali - As Mali continues to face a series of economic and security challenges, community, religious, and traditional leaders are calling on citizens to remain vigilant, united, and resilient in support of…
title_en: Malians Urged to Show Resilience and Unity Amid National Crisis
excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali - As Mali continues to face a series of economic and security challenges, community, religious, and traditional leaders are calling on citizens to remain vigilant, united, and resilient in support of…
body_en:
Bamako, Mali - As Mali continues to face a series of economic and security challenges, community, religious, and traditional leaders are calling on citizens to remain vigilant, united, and resilient in support of national stability.

Speaking on behalf of the founding families of Niaré, Touré, and Dravé, Mamoutou Niaré, interim patriarch of the Niaré family, urged Malians to stay steadfast and supportive of government efforts to overcome the current crisis.

“We must know where we are going, ignore distractions, and protect our leaders,” he said. “Those who have lost loved ones or possessions have sacrificed for the nation. Let us honor them through resilience and unity.”

He also appealed to traditional authorities to encourage Malians to “tighten their belts” and remain engaged in efforts to restore peace across the country.

Echoing similar sentiments, Reverend Dr. Nouh Ag Infa Yattara, General Delegate of the Evangelical Protestant Church of Mali (AGEMPEM), praised the population’s resilience and called for renewed patriotism and solidarity.

“These hardships are temporary. We commend the authorities for their efforts to address challenges in fuel, electricity, and security,” he said, adding that the church is dedicating prayers and fasting “for peace and national recovery.”

Jonas Dembélé, President of the Episcopal Conference of Mali, also urged Catholics to remain steadfast in prayer and action for peace.

“Let us ask God to make Mali a land of justice and peace,” he said. “The Bishops invite all Christian communities to persevere in prayer and to become peacemakers, advocates of justice, forgiveness, and reconciliation.”

Meanwhile, Chief Commissioner Panama Dembélé, Commander of the Road Traffic Group, commended citizens for their patience during the ongoing fuel shortage, urging continued civic discipline at fuel stations.

“We thank the population for its resilience and cooperation,” he said. “Respecting the order of arrival at fuel stations will help avoid congestion and allow emergency vehicles to operate freely.”

He reassured the public that the authorities are taking all necessary measures to find a lasting solution to the crisis.

title: US, UK Pull Embassy Staff from Mali as Security Situation Worsens
excerpt: Bamako, Mali - The United States and the United Kingdom have withdrawn non-essential embassy staff from Mali as the country grapples with an escalating security crisis marked by a terrorist-led fuel blockade, widespread…
title_en: US, UK Pull Embassy Staff from Mali as Security Situation Worsens
excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali - The United States and the United Kingdom have withdrawn non-essential embassy staff from Mali as the country grapples with an escalating security crisis marked by a terrorist-led fuel blockade, widespread…
body_en:
Bamako, Mali - The United States and the United Kingdom have withdrawn non-essential embassy staff from Mali as the country grapples with an escalating security crisis marked by a terrorist-led fuel blockade, widespread shortages, and growing instability around the capital.

The US State Department on Thursday ordered the departure of “non-emergency employees and their family members” from the embassy in Bamako, citing increased safety risks. The move followed a Security Alert issued on October 28, which urged all American citizens in Mali to “depart immediately using commercial aviation.”

According to the alert, persistent infrastructure breakdowns, nationwide fuel shortages, and the closure of public institutions - including schools and universities - have severely disrupted normal life. Meanwhile, clashes between Malian forces and jihadist groups near Bamako have heightened fears of further violence.

“The international airport in Bamako remains open and flights are available,” the alert stated. “Overland routes to neighboring countries may not be safe due to terrorist attacks along national highways.”

title: Mali Hosts 16th WCO-WCA Regional Customs Intelligence Meeting
excerpt: BAMAKO, MALI - Mali has once again demonstrated its assertive regional leadership by hosting the 16th Annual Meeting of National Liaison Officers from the World Customs Organization (WCO) offices responsible for…
title_en: Mali Hosts 16th WCO-WCA Regional Customs Intelligence Meeting
excerpt_en: BAMAKO, MALI - Mali has once again demonstrated its assertive regional leadership by hosting the 16th Annual Meeting of National Liaison Officers from the World Customs Organization (WCO) offices responsible for…
body_en:
BAMAKO, MALI - Mali has once again demonstrated its assertive regional leadership by hosting the 16th Annual Meeting of National Liaison Officers from the World Customs Organization (WCO) offices responsible for intelligence in West and Central Africa. The five-day conference opened on Monday, November 3, 2025, in Bamako under the theme: “Fragile Borders and Optimizing Customs Revenue in the West and Central African WCO Region: Challenges and Prospects.”

The gathering brings together customs intelligence officials to strengthen cooperation and share data aimed at countering illicit trafficking, smuggling, commercial fraud, and terrorism financing - persistent threats undermining the region’s security and economic growth.

Colonel-Major Ahmadou Sanogo, Director of Intelligence and the Fight Against Fraud of Malian Customs, highlighted the central role of intelligence in border control. “Without effective collection, analysis, and dissemination of intelligence, no policy of control or fight against fraud can produce lasting results,” he said. He emphasized that African customs agencies are modernizing their systems through stronger human and technical capacities, open-source intelligence, and enhanced cross-border cooperation.

Echoing this, Ibrahim Njoya, Director of the Regional Liaison Office for Central Africa, praised the WCO’s framework that enables the collection, processing, and dissemination of high-quality customs intelligence to curb fraud and illegal trade across the region.

Representing the WCO Secretary-General, Ousmane Coundoul described this year’s theme as “undeniably relevant,” noting that customs administrations have a dual responsibility - to protect borders and to foster economic prosperity.

Inspector General Amadou Konaté, Director General of Malian Customs and Vice-President of the WCO West and Central Africa Region, acknowledged significant progress but stressed that challenges remain. “Despite numerous seizures of weapons, ammunition, drugs, and dual-use goods, much remains to be done,” he said.

Participants are expected to produce a set of recommendations to strengthen customs intelligence collaboration and enhance revenue collection across member states. The Bamako meeting underscores Mali’s commitment to regional security, good governance, and economic resilience - values that continue to shape its growing influence in West and Central Africa.
