title: Mali Council of Ministers Adopts New Regulations for Architects and Makes Key Appointments
excerpt: Bamako, Mali - The Council of Ministers of Mali convened on Wednesday, November 5, 2025, at the Koulouba Palace under the chairmanship of General Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition and Head of State.
title_en: Mali Council of Ministers Adopts New Regulations for Architects and Makes Key Appointments
excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali - The Council of Ministers of Mali convened on Wednesday, November 5, 2025, at the Koulouba Palace under the chairmanship of General Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition and Head of State.
body_en:
Bamako, Mali - The Council of Ministers of Mali convened on Wednesday, November 5, 2025, at the Koulouba Palace under the chairmanship of General Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition and Head of State. The meeting resulted in the adoption of new draft texts governing the profession of architects, a series of key appointments, and several important government communications.

On the proposal of the Minister of Urban Planning, Housing, Domains, Territorial Development, and Population, the Council adopted new regulations aligning Mali’s architecture profession with West African Economic and Monetary Union (UEMOA) standards.The reforms allow architects from UEMOA member states to freely practice in Mali, introduce a 24-month mandatory professional internship, and establish Regional Councils and a Government Commissioner to the Order of Architects.

Several high-level appointments were made across ministries:

Defense and Veterans Affairs: Colonel-Major Boubacar Yassanry Sanogoh was named Director of Joint Higher Defence Studies at the War College of Mali.

Reconciliation, Peace and National Cohesion: Mamadou Fane was appointed Secretary General, with Chief Police Controller Sory Ibrahim Ousmane Sidibe as Technical Advisor.

Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation: Major General Ibrahima Dahirou Dembele was named Ambassador to Saudi Arabia.

Economy and Finance: Aly Boubacar Cissé became Paymaster General of the Treasury, with Amadou Camara, Ibrahim Coulibaly, and Niarga Keita appointed to key Treasury roles.

Agriculture: Bréhima Sogoba was appointed National Director of Rural Engineering, and Bourama Dembele became CEO of the Land Development and Irrigation Water Supply Agency.

Livestock and Fisheries: Mamadou Traoré was named National Coordinator of the Sustainable Development Project for Pastoral Farms in the Sahel.

Cybercrime Convention: Mali participated in the UN Convention against Cybercrime signing in Hanoi, Vietnam, reaffirming its commitment to global digital security.

Lomé Peace and Security Forum: Malian officials called for greater strategic autonomy and solidarity for the Sahel region.

Non-Aligned Movement Meeting: Mali reiterated its commitment to peace and sovereignty while denouncing foreign support to terrorist groups.

Aswan Forum: The Foreign Minister represented Mali at discussions on Sahel cooperation and bilateral relations.

Additionally, the Minister of Health and Social Development reported a rise in dengue cases, prompting the Head of State to call for stricter public health measures.

title: France Urges Citizens to Leave Mali Amid Jihadist-Imposed Fuel Blockade
excerpt: Bamako, Mali - France has urged its citizens in Mali to leave the country “as soon as possible” as Islamist insurgents continue to enforce a fuel blockade that has crippled daily life across the nation.
title_en: France Urges Citizens to Leave Mali Amid Jihadist-Imposed Fuel Blockade
excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali - France has urged its citizens in Mali to leave the country “as soon as possible” as Islamist insurgents continue to enforce a fuel blockade that has crippled daily life across the nation.
body_en:
Bamako, Mali - France has urged its citizens in Mali to leave the country “as soon as possible” as Islamist insurgents continue to enforce a fuel blockade that has crippled daily life across the nation.

In a statement issued by the French Foreign Ministry, Paris advised its nationals to depart using available commercial flights and to avoid overland travel, citing mounting insecurity and growing logistical challenges.

The warning comes amid a two-month blockade orchestrated by Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), an al-Qaeda-affiliated militant group that has attacked fuel convoys and tankers on major supply routes, effectively cutting off the landlocked country from vital imports.

The blockade has disrupted transportation, electricity, and trade in Bamako and other regions, worsening living conditions and sparking concerns over the government’s ability to manage the crisis.

Adding to the turmoil, Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC)-the world’s largest shipping line-announced it was suspending operations in Mali, citing security risks and the blockade’s impact on logistics.

Mali, which relies entirely on overland fuel imports from neighboring countries such as Senegal and Côte d’Ivoire, has been under a military junta led by General Assimi Goïta since 2020. The government came to power promising to restore security after years of conflict involving separatist groups and Islamist insurgents.

However, the withdrawal of French forces and UN peacekeepers, alongside the arrival of Russian paramilitary contractors, has not curbed the violence. Vast areas of the north and east remain beyond state control.

Last month, the U.S. Embassy in Bamako ordered the departure of non-essential staff and their families, warning that the fuel shortage could further destabilize the country and “disrupt the overall security situation in unpredictable ways.”

As conditions worsen, international observers fear the blockade could deepen Mali’s humanitarian crisis and further isolate the junta-led government from its foreign partners.

Economy and Tech.

title: Mali’s BNDA Secures $40 Million IFC Loan to Boost Agricultural Lending
excerpt: Bamako, Mali - The Banque Nationale de Développement Agricole (BNDA) has secured a $40 million loan from the International Finance Corporation (IFC) to expand lending to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the…
title_en: Mali’s BNDA Secures $40 Million IFC Loan to Boost Agricultural Lending
excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali - The Banque Nationale de Développement Agricole (BNDA) has secured a $40 million loan from the International Finance Corporation (IFC) to expand lending to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the…
body_en:
Bamako, Mali - The Banque Nationale de Développement Agricole (BNDA) has secured a $40 million loan from the International Finance Corporation (IFC) to expand lending to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the agricultural sector. The agreement, announced on October 30, 2025, aims to strengthen financing for smallholder farmers, cooperatives, and agribusinesses across Mali.

The IFC package also includes an additional $10 million trade finance facility, designed to facilitate the import and export of essential agricultural goods and inputs.

Under the five-year program, BNDA plans to grow its SME loan portfolio to more than $270 million, channeling funds toward women-led businesses and climate-smart agribusiness projects. About 25 percent of the loans will target women-owned enterprises, while 10 percent will be reserved for projects promoting renewable energy, sustainable irrigation, and green agriculture.

According to IFC estimates, the partnership could expand BNDA’s green financing portfolio by 90 percent and create between 8,600 and 14,200 jobs - both direct and indirect - over the next five years.

“This partnership with IFC will enable us to increase our support for farmers, SMEs, and women entrepreneurs across the country,” said Badara Aliou Coulibaly, BNDA’s Managing Director. “It will also allow us to integrate digital and sustainable solutions, expanding access to finance and reinforcing national food security.”

Beyond financial support, the IFC will provide technical assistance to help BNDA strengthen its agricultural lending strategy, risk management systems, and gender inclusion framework. The program will also introduce customized credit scoring tools to improve access to loans for small businesses and cooperatives.

The deal comes as Mali seeks to revitalize an agricultural sector that employs nearly 70 percent of its population but contributes only 38 percent of GDP. Most farms remain small-scale - averaging 4.8 hectares - and face chronic challenges such as limited irrigation, low yields, and underinvestment in modern production systems.

The IFC’s intervention is expected to bolster the sector’s resilience and productivity, aligning with Mali’s broader goal of achieving food security and inclusive economic growth.

title: Mali Launches Advanced Drought Monitoring System to Protect Agriculture
excerpt: Bamako, Mali - In response to growing concerns over recurring droughts that threaten food security and rural livelihoods, Mali has introduced a new digital platform designed to track and analyze drought conditions in real time.
title_en: Mali Launches Advanced Drought Monitoring System to Protect Agriculture
excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali - In response to growing concerns over recurring droughts that threaten food security and rural livelihoods, Mali has introduced a new digital platform designed to track and analyze drought conditions in real time.
body_en:
Bamako, Mali - In response to growing concerns over recurring droughts that threaten food security and rural livelihoods, Mali has introduced a new digital platform designed to track and analyze drought conditions in real time. The Mali Drought Monitoring System (MaliDMS) aims to strengthen early warning capacities and support data-driven decision-making for agricultural resilience.

Droughts remain one of the most severe natural hazards affecting Mali’s economy and food production. The National Directorate of Agriculture (Direction Nationale de l’Agriculture, DNA) has long stressed the urgent need for a reliable monitoring system to identify drought-affected areas and evaluate their impact on key crops. The initiative seeks to improve the accuracy of national agricultural statistics and help authorities craft targeted policies to mitigate the effects of water scarcity.

Developed using Water Productivity through Open-access Remotely sensed data (WaPOR) from FAO and other high-resolution satellite sources, the MaliDMS provides near real-time assessments of drought onset, duration, and severity. Its interactive interface displays dynamic maps and graphs that visualize changes in precipitation, vegetation health, and soil moisture, giving policymakers and farmers a clearer picture of evolving drought conditions.

MaliDMS employs Level 1 WaPOR data with a spatial resolution of 300 meters, updated every 10 days, to deliver detailed insights on indicators such as actual and reference evapotranspiration (AETI and RET), precipitation (P), and net primary production (NPP). These datasets enable national, regional, and local assessments of drought impact.

Users can access, analyze, and download results in multiple formats, with the platform available in both English and French. By integrating advanced satellite analytics with open data principles, MaliDMS represents a significant step toward improving drought preparedness and safeguarding agricultural productivity across the country.

title: President Assimi Goïta Inaugurates Mali’s Second Lithium Mine to Boost Economic Sovereignty
excerpt: Bougouni, Mali - On Monday, November 3, 2025, President of the Transition, General Assimi Goïta, officially inaugurated the Bougouni Lithium Mines SA (LMLB SA), Mali’s second operational lithium mine.
title_en: President Assimi Goïta Inaugurates Mali’s Second Lithium Mine to Boost Economic Sovereignty
excerpt_en: Bougouni, Mali - On Monday, November 3, 2025, President of the Transition, General Assimi Goïta, officially inaugurated the Bougouni Lithium Mines SA (LMLB SA), Mali’s second operational lithium mine.
body_en:
Bougouni, Mali - On Monday, November 3, 2025, President of the Transition, General Assimi Goïta, officially inaugurated the Bougouni Lithium Mines SA (LMLB SA), Mali’s second operational lithium mine. The event highlights the Transitional Government’s determination to strengthen economic sovereignty and leverage the country’s natural resources despite a complex security and geopolitical environment.

The Bougouni mine represents a key milestone in Mali’s ambitious policy of resource-driven, inclusive, and sustainable growth. Positioned in the Bougouni region, the project aims to transform the nation’s rich lithium reserves into a driver of local development and global energy participation. Lithium, essential for batteries in electric vehicles, smartphones, and energy storage, places Mali among countries actively contributing to the energy transition.

The Bougouni Lithium Mines SA project is structured in two main phases. The first phase at the N'Gouanala site, already underway, involves a $65 million investment and will produce nearly 120,000 tons of lithium concentrate annually over four years. The second phase, scheduled for 2028, will expand operations to the Sogola-Baoulé and Boumou sites, requiring $180 million in investment and increasing production to over 200,000 tons per year. In total, $245 million (over 150 billion CFA francs) will be invested, reflecting strong investor confidence in Mali’s stability and governance.

The mine employs advanced, environmentally friendly technologies to ensure efficient extraction while minimizing ecological impact. The project’s operations will create jobs, improve local infrastructure, and support community development through education, health services, and local entrepreneurship initiatives.

The Malian state holds a 35% stake in the company, including a 10% free share under the new Mining Code, ensuring fair distribution of wealth and long-term benefits. Revenues for Mali are projected at over $380 million (approximately 230 billion CFA francs) from taxes, royalties, and dividends. Beyond financial gains, the project will generate direct and indirect employment, develop regional infrastructure, and empower local communities.

The inauguration of the Bougouni Lithium Mines SA underscores Mali’s commitment to economic autonomy. By focusing on local value creation and responsible management, the government aims to make natural resources a catalyst for national transformation. The project exemplifies state-investor partnerships based on transparency, social responsibility, and sustainable growth.

The Bougouni mine represents both a national pride and a strategic vision for Mali. By responsibly developing lithium resources, the country is positioning itself as a key player in the global energy transition while ensuring that benefits accrue primarily to its citizens. The mine will contribute to long-term economic stability, technological advancement, and community empowerment, reaffirming Mali’s path toward economic, technological, and energy sovereignty.

title: A Message of Firmness and Reassurance: Diop Calms Foreign Partners Amid Mali’s Fuel and Security Challenges
excerpt: Bamako, Mali - Amid growing concerns over security and fuel shortages, Mali’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Abdoulaye Diop, has sought to reassure the country’s foreign partners, affirming the government’s firm…
title_en: A Message of Firmness and Reassurance: Diop Calms Foreign Partners Amid Mali’s Fuel and Security Challenges
excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali - Amid growing concerns over security and fuel shortages, Mali’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Abdoulaye Diop, has sought to reassure the country’s foreign partners, affirming the government’s firm…
body_en:
Bamako, Mali - Amid growing concerns over security and fuel shortages, Mali’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Abdoulaye Diop, has sought to reassure the country’s foreign partners, affirming the government’s firm commitment to restoring stability.

As several embassies in Bamako advised staff to take precautionary measures, Diop outlined the strong actions taken by Mali’s transitional authorities to address the crisis. He reminded that Mali, having faced a decade-long hybrid conflict, has developed significant resilience and the capacity to manage complex challenges.

The minister paid tribute to the Malian Armed Forces and the Sahel Joint Force, commending their daily efforts to defend the nation and maintain the supply of fuel despite mounting pressures.

Responding to criticism of Mali’s choice of international partners in the fight against terrorism, Diop reaffirmed Bamako’s openness to cooperation with all nations that respect its sovereignty. He dismissed claims of a fuel “shortage” or “blockade,” calling the situation artificial and emphasizing that the government had taken “all necessary measures” through the inter-ministerial crisis management committee.

Diplomatic representatives accredited to Mali expressed satisfaction following their discussions with the minister. Igor Gromyko, Russia’s ambassador and dean of the diplomatic corps, reiterated his support for Mali.

U.S. Ambassador Rachna Korhonen also saluted the courage and determination of Malian forces in confronting terrorism, reaffirming Washington’s solidarity with the Malian people. Similarly, Spain’s ambassador, Antonio Guillén Hidalgo, welcomed the “decisive measures” taken by the government, while the ambassadors of Burkina Faso and Niger praised the resilience and unity of the Malian people, describing them as “a foresighted nation that has not wavered.”

title: Mali Closes Schools as Fuel Blockade by Armed Group Paralyzes the Country
excerpt: Bamako, Mali - Mali’s military government has ordered a two-week nationwide closure of schools and universities as the country reels from the economic paralysis caused by an ongoing fuel blockade imposed by jihadist…
title_en: Mali Closes Schools as Fuel Blockade by Armed Group Paralyzes the Country
excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali - Mali’s military government has ordered a two-week nationwide closure of schools and universities as the country reels from the economic paralysis caused by an ongoing fuel blockade imposed by jihadist…
body_en:
Bamako, Mali - Mali’s military government has ordered a two-week nationwide closure of schools and universities as the country reels from the economic paralysis caused by an ongoing fuel blockade imposed by jihadist fighters linked to al-Qaeda.

The announcement, made on Sunday, October 26, 2025, by Education Minister Amadou Sy Savane, cited disruptions in fuel supply that have crippled transportation across the landlocked nation.

“The suspension until November 9 is due to disruptions in fuel supplies affecting the movement of school staff,” Savane said, adding that authorities are “doing everything possible” to restore normal supplies before classes resume on November 10.

A statement from the Interministerial Committee for Crisis and Disaster Management confirmed that fuel restrictions would remain in place “until further notice,” with priority at petrol stations given to emergency services, public transport, and essential assistance vehicles.

The blockade, declared nearly two months ago by Jama’at Nusrat ul-Islam wa al-Muslimin (JNIM) - an al-Qaeda affiliate operating across the Sahel - has severely disrupted fuel imports from Senegal and Ivory Coast, Mali’s key trade corridors.

JNIM claimed the blockade was retaliation for government restrictions on the sale of fuel outside official stations in rural areas - a measure aimed at cutting off the group’s supply routes.

The embargo has pushed Mali’s already fragile economy to the brink. Long queues now stretch for kilometers at gas stations in Bamako and other cities, while public transport, commerce, and electricity supply have been heavily affected. Prices of basic goods have soared, and several private businesses have temporarily suspended operations.

Mali’s reliance on fuel imports - vital for its power generation, transportation, and agriculture sectors - has magnified the crisis. The landlocked nation imports nearly all its petroleum products, making it especially vulnerable to border disruptions.

For more than a decade, Mali and its neighbors Burkina Faso and Niger have faced persistent attacks from armed groups affiliated with al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS). Following successive coups in all three countries, the new juntas expelled French forces and sought security cooperation with Russian Wagner mercenaries - a move analysts say has yielded limited success.

Observers note that the ongoing fuel blockade poses one of the most serious tests yet for Mali’s military rulers, who seized power in 2020 promising to restore security and stabilize the economy.

“The blockade is a major setback for the junta,” said one Bamako-based analyst. “It has exposed the regime’s vulnerability and its inability to secure key trade routes despite promises to end the crisis.”

As the fuel crisis deepens, public frustration is growing - even as authorities tighten control over dissent and call for national resilience amid the escalating humanitarian strain.

title: Mali Settles 30-Year Dispute Over Voluntary Retirements (1986-1993)
excerpt: BAMAKO, MALI - After three decades of waiting, the Government of Mali has authorized the payment of benefits and compensation to former public servants who voluntarily retired between 1986 and 1993 under the country’s…
title_en: Mali Settles 30-Year Dispute Over Voluntary Retirements (1986-1993)
excerpt_en: BAMAKO, MALI - After three decades of waiting, the Government of Mali has authorized the payment of benefits and compensation to former public servants who voluntarily retired between 1986 and 1993 under the country’s…
body_en:
BAMAKO, MALI - After three decades of waiting, the Government of Mali has authorized the payment of benefits and compensation to former public servants who voluntarily retired between 1986 and 1993 under the country’s structural adjustment program. The decision was formalized through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed on Tuesday, November 4, 2025, between the Government and the National Union of Workers of Mali (UNTM).

“It is with deep emotion and a real sense of accomplishment that I speak on this solemn occasion,” declared Yacouba Katilé, Secretary General of the UNTM, highlighting the significance of this long-awaited social justice measure.

The agreement marks the end of a protracted struggle that began when thousands of civil servants accepted voluntary retirement during a period of severe economic austerity. Many were left without due compensation for decades. The new MoU reflects the transitional government’s commitment to justice, fairness, and social cohesion.

According to Dr. Fassoun Coulibaly, Minister of Labour, Public Service, and Social Dialogue, the commission handling the case focused on three key components:

Reimbursement of the employer’s 8% contribution share;

Preservation of pension rights for 61 employees who had completed 15 years of service.

To settle the issue, the government has allocated over nine billion CFA francs, an act described by Katilé as both “moral and social redress.” “By signing this protocol, we are taking an act of justice toward these former workers who contributed their sweat and loyalty to the building of Mali,” he stated.

The agreement includes a three-year payment moratorium, with compensation to be deposited directly into the individual accounts of the beneficiaries. This landmark decision not only closes a painful chapter in Mali’s labor history but also signals the government’s determination to restore trust and equity between the state and its workforce.

title: Mali Court Jails Former Prime Minister Moussa Mara Over Social Media Post
excerpt: Bamako, Mali - A court in Mali has sentenced former Prime Minister Moussa Mara to one year in prison over a social media post expressing solidarity with political prisoners, in a ruling that has drawn sharp criticism…
title_en: Mali Court Jails Former Prime Minister Moussa Mara Over Social Media Post
excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali - A court in Mali has sentenced former Prime Minister Moussa Mara to one year in prison over a social media post expressing solidarity with political prisoners, in a ruling that has drawn sharp criticism…
body_en:
Bamako, Mali - A court in Mali has sentenced former Prime Minister Moussa Mara to one year in prison over a social media post expressing solidarity with political prisoners, in a ruling that has drawn sharp criticism from human rights groups.

The National Cybercrime Centre Court in Bamako found Mara guilty on Monday, October 27, 2025, of “undermining the credibility of the state and opposing legitimate authority.” In addition to his one-year prison term without parole, the court imposed a 12-month suspended sentence and a fine of 500,000 CFA francs (about $887).

Mara, 50, who served as Prime Minister from 2014 to 2015, was arrested on August 1 after publishing a post on X (formerly Twitter) in which he named several detained political figures and declared his “unwavering solidarity with prisoners of conscience.”

“As long as the night lasts, the sun will appear,” he wrote on July 4. “We will fight by all means for this to happen as soon as possible.”

His legal team denounced the sentence as unjust and confirmed plans to appeal.

“The judicial battle does not end today,” Mara’s lawyers said in a statement. “It continues with the same determination, on the grounds of law and truth.”

A close associate of Mara, speaking anonymously, said the decision was expected but “made no sense,” adding: “Tell me what his crime is.”

Mali has been under military rule since 2020, when General Assimi Goïta seized power following two consecutive coups. Despite pledges to return the country to civilian governance by 2024, elections have been repeatedly postponed. Earlier this year, the junta dissolved political parties and extended Goïta’s mandate by five years.

Amnesty International condemned the ruling as a “travesty of justice,” urging the authorities to end their “escalating repression of peaceful dissent” and to release individuals detained for expressing their opinions.

The conviction marks one of the most high-profile prosecutions of a political figure since the junta took power and reflects what observers describe as tightening restrictions on free expression in Mali.

title: Critic of Mali’s Junta Forcibly Disappeared in Bamako
excerpt: BAMAKO, MALI - Concerns are mounting over the fate of Cheick Oumar Diallo, a well-known critic of Mali’s military junta and former trade unionist, who was forcibly taken by gendarmes in Bamako on October 25 and has not…
title_en: Critic of Mali’s Junta Forcibly Disappeared in Bamako
excerpt_en: BAMAKO, MALI - Concerns are mounting over the fate of Cheick Oumar Diallo, a well-known critic of Mali’s military junta and former trade unionist, who was forcibly taken by gendarmes in Bamako on October 25 and has not…
body_en:
BAMAKO, MALI - Concerns are mounting over the fate of Cheick Oumar Diallo, a well-known critic of Mali’s military junta and former trade unionist, who was forcibly taken by gendarmes in Bamako on October 25 and has not been seen since.

According to witnesses, four gendarmes arrived in a pickup truck and on motorbikes while Diallo was speaking with friends in the capital. They informed him that they had orders to arrest him but gave no reason. When Diallo attempted to flee, he fell into a ditch and injured his leg before being seized, thrown into the truck, and driven away.

Diallo’s colleagues have searched police and gendarmerie stations across Bamako but have been unable to locate him. They believe his disappearance is linked to his activism and outspoken criticism of the junta.

A former employee of the national water company, Diallo was a member of its autonomous union and a whistleblower. In July 2024, he published a letter alleging that Mali’s drinking water was unsafe. He was arrested soon afterward and later dismissed from his position following his release in May 2025.

Mali’s junta has repeatedly targeted trade unionists and critics since seizing power in 2021. In June 2024, the secretary-general of Mali’s main bank union, Hamadoun Bah, was arrested on charges seen as politically motivated, sparking a five-day strike before his release.

Human rights observers say Diallo’s case bears the hallmarks of an enforced disappearance-an arrest carried out without acknowledgment or information on the detainee’s whereabouts-placing him outside legal protection. Such disappearances violate international laws prohibiting arbitrary detention, torture, and extrajudicial killings.

Mali is a signatory to the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance, ratified in 2009.

Rights advocates and colleagues are calling on the Malian authorities to immediately disclose Diallo’s location, ensure his safety, and end their campaign of intimidation against trade unionists and government critics.

title: Mali on the Brink as al-Qaida-Linked Jihadists Tighten Grip on the Country
excerpt: Bamako, Mali - The al-Qaida-affiliated jihadist group Jama’at Nusrat ul-Islam wa al-Muslimin (JNIM) is intensifying its offensive across Mali, blocking key supply routes and deepening a crisis that has brought the…
title_en: Mali on the Brink as al-Qaida-Linked Jihadists Tighten Grip on the Country
excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali - The al-Qaida-affiliated jihadist group Jama’at Nusrat ul-Islam wa al-Muslimin (JNIM) is intensifying its offensive across Mali, blocking key supply routes and deepening a crisis that has brought the…
body_en:
Bamako, Mali - The al-Qaida-affiliated jihadist group Jama’at Nusrat ul-Islam wa al-Muslimin (JNIM) is intensifying its offensive across Mali, blocking key supply routes and deepening a crisis that has brought the nation to the verge of economic paralysis and political collapse.

Over the past two weeks, JNIM fighters have attacked fuel convoys and blocked major roads leading to Bamako and other regions, cutting off fuel imports from neighboring Ivory Coast, Mauritania, and Senegal. The blockade has triggered a severe fuel shortage that has left the capital struggling with long queues at petrol stations, power cuts, and rising food prices.

With schools closed, shops shuttered, and public transport largely halted, daily life in Bamako has come to a near standstill. The disruption has worsened an already fragile political climate under the transitional government led by the military junta.

Analysts warn that the militants are tightening their hold around the capital. In areas under JNIM control, residents have reported the enforcement of strict dress codes and religious rulings through makeshift courts that lack fair-trial guarantees, according to a 2024 Human Rights Watch report.

Western governments have raised the alarm. The United States this week issued two security advisories urging its citizens to leave Mali “immediately,” citing the deteriorating security situation. Australia, Germany, and Italy issued similar warnings.

A former Malian minister, now in exile, told The Guardian that the country risks “collapsing before our eyes,” warning of the potential for another coup - Mali’s third in five years and sixth since independence in 1960.

“Before 31 December, a coup will happen in the Sahel,” the former official said. “Mali will go first, and then the same domino effect could follow, just like between 2020 and 2023.”

Experts say the coming weeks will be decisive. Ulf Laessing, head of the Sahel Programme at Germany’s Konrad Adenauer Foundation, said the situation could worsen as remaining fuel reserves are depleted.

“Next week will be really bad,” he warned. “It’s difficult to see how they can resupply the capital in sufficient quantities.”

Observers fear that if Bamako were to fall, Mali could face the grim prospect of an Islamist republic under JNIM, mirroring Taliban-ruled Afghanistan - a development that could destabilize the entire Sahel region.

title: Mali’s Fragile Regime Confronts Rising Islamist Threat and Internal Strains
excerpt: Bamako, Mali - Mali faces a precarious crossroads as a deepening insurgency and a worsening fuel crisis compound the challenges confronting the country’s military government.
title_en: Mali’s Fragile Regime Confronts Rising Islamist Threat and Internal Strains
excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali - Mali faces a precarious crossroads as a deepening insurgency and a worsening fuel crisis compound the challenges confronting the country’s military government.
body_en:
Bamako, Mali - Mali faces a precarious crossroads as a deepening insurgency and a worsening fuel crisis compound the challenges confronting the country’s military government. Analysts warn that the collapse of the junta could create a vacuum exploited by Islamist groups seeking to establish an Islamic state.

According to Ulf Laessing, head of the Sahel Programme at Germany’s Konrad Adenauer Foundation, popular unrest has been muted largely due to fear of what might follow."So far nobody is demonstrating against the government because people know that if they bring it down, the next one could be an Islamist regime," Laessing said. "That fear is, paradoxically, helping to strengthen the junta’s hold on power."

Mali’s political turmoil began in June 2020 with the emergence of the June 5 Movement - Rally of Patriotic Forces (M5-RFP), a coalition of civil society groups, opposition parties, and religious leaders. The coalition led mass protests against then-President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta, accusing his administration of corruption and failing to curb jihadist violence.

Imam Mahmoud Dicko, a prominent and polarizing cleric, played a leading role in mobilizing the demonstrations. Dicko first gained national attention during the 1991 uprising that toppled President Moussa Traoré.

During mediation talks led by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), Keïta reportedly warned that Dicko sought to turn Mali into an Islamic state under sharia law - a claim that triggered a heated reaction among regional leaders.

Weeks later, soldiers led by then-Captain Assimi Goïta overthrew Keïta’s government. A second coup in 2021 cemented Goïta’s authority, installing him as President of the Transition.

The junta initially pledged to restore civilian rule through elections in February 2022, but the process has been repeatedly delayed. Meanwhile, violence has surged.

Data from the Africa Center for Strategic Studies indicate that more than 17,700 people have been killed in Mali’s conflict since 2012, with over two-thirds of those deaths occurring after 2020. The al-Qaida-affiliated group JNIM has expanded operations beyond Mali into Benin and Nigeria, fueled in part by ransom payments from high-profile kidnappings.

Human rights organizations accuse Malian forces, allied militias, and Russian Wagner mercenaries of committing widespread abuses during counterinsurgency operations.

title: Mali: JNIM Frees Three Hostages After Record $50 Million Ransom and Arms Exchange Amid Capital Embargo
excerpt: Bamako, Mali - Three foreign nationals held by the Al-Qaeda-linked jihadist group JNIM in Mali have been released following a record ransom and arms exchange, highlighting the group’s growing influence amid the…
title_en: Mali: JNIM Frees Three Hostages After Record $50 Million Ransom and Arms Exchange Amid Capital Embargo
excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali - Three foreign nationals held by the Al-Qaeda-linked jihadist group JNIM in Mali have been released following a record ransom and arms exchange, highlighting the group’s growing influence amid the…
body_en:
Bamako, Mali - Three foreign nationals held by the Al-Qaeda-linked jihadist group JNIM in Mali have been released following a record ransom and arms exchange, highlighting the group’s growing influence amid the country’s ongoing security crisis.

The hostages-two Emirati citizens, including retired General Joumaa bin Maktoum al-Maktoum, a member of Dubai’s ruling family and a gold trader, and an Iranian national-were abducted in Bamako on 23 September. They were freed on 29 October near the northern city of Gao, after more than a month in captivity, in exchange for at least $50 million and several tonnes of ammunition, according to security sources.

The previous hostages were typically ransomed for $6-10 million. Joumaa bin Maktoum al-Maktoum’s high-profile capture allowed JNIM to command an unprecedented price. The other two hostages included a Pakistani man, initially thought to be Emirati, and the Iranian national.

JNIM, which has shifted its focus from targeting Western nationals to countries it considers supporters of the Malian, Burkinabe, and Nigerien regimes, currently holds a range of foreign nationals, including Chinese, Indians, Ukrainians associated with Wagner, an Iranian, and Egyptians, whose connections to Malian authorities are reportedly under scrutiny.

The ransom comes amid JNIM’s continued embargo on fuel imports to the Malian capital, Bamako, in effect since early September. The blockade has triggered a severe gasoline shortage, paralyzing the economy, and hundreds of tanker trucks coming from Abidjan and Dakar have been set ablaze by the group. JNIM has stated that its ultimate goal is to destabilize the Malian authorities-who seized power in the 2020 and 2021 coups-and establish Islamic governance.

Negotiations for the hostages, believed to have been mediated through secret channels, underscore the growing financial and political leverage of jihadist groups in Mali, where abductions have become a lucrative source of funding amid ongoing insecurity and political instability.

title: Malian Military Secures Fuel Convoy, Pledges to Prevent Future Attacks
excerpt: Bamako, Mali - The Malian military has successfully thwarted an attack on a strategic fuel convoy, assuring citizens that measures are in place to prevent further disruptions to the country’s energy supply.
title_en: Malian Military Secures Fuel Convoy, Pledges to Prevent Future Attacks
excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali - The Malian military has successfully thwarted an attack on a strategic fuel convoy, assuring citizens that measures are in place to prevent further disruptions to the country’s energy supply.
body_en:
Bamako, Mali - The Malian military has successfully thwarted an attack on a strategic fuel convoy, assuring citizens that measures are in place to prevent further disruptions to the country’s energy supply.

On Sunday, October 26, 2025, the Malian Armed Forces (FAMa) launched an operation in the Bougouni region, neutralizing dozens of armed terrorists who were preparing to target a fuel convoy. The operation, carried out under the command of General Oumar Diarra, was hailed for its speed, professionalism, and coordination, allowing the convoy to resume its journey and securing vital fuel supplies for Bamako and other regions.

The attack had contributed to an ongoing fuel shortage in the capital and across Mali, which authorities attribute to external terrorist pressures seeking to destabilize the country’s economy. Military officials emphasized that the government remains committed to protecting national resources and maintaining sovereignty against foreign exploitation.

“The speculation and external pressure will not deter us. The sovereignty of our country cannot be compromised,” a statement from the General Staff said. Authorities confirmed that they are taking decisive steps to secure fuel supplies, diversify partnerships, and safeguard Mali’s economic stability.

The operation in Kolondiéba highlights the Malian Armed Forces’ continued efforts to combat terrorism and protect critical infrastructure, ensuring the uninterrupted delivery of essential resources to citizens.

Conclusion : Mali at a Critical Crossroads (Oct. 25 - Nov. 8, 2025)

The period between October 25 and November 8, 2025, reveals a Mali operating under immense pressure from both external threats and internal political and economic reforms. The country is simultaneously asserting its national sovereignty and regional leadership while grappling with a severe, existential security and humanitarian crisis.

The most immediate challenge remains the crippling fuel blockade imposed by the al-Qaeda-linked Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM). This blockade has severely disrupted daily life, leading to the nationwide closure of schools and universities , rising food prices, and economic paralysis. The crisis prompted the withdrawal of non-essential embassy staff by the United States and the United Kingdom, with France also urging its citizens to leave immediately. The release of three foreign hostages, including a member of Dubai's ruling family, for a record $50 million ransom and arms exchange further underscored JNIM's growing financial and political leverage.

In response to the escalating crisis, Malian authorities are focusing on twin strategies:

Security Mobilization: The Malian Armed Forces (FAMa) successfully secured a strategic fuel convoy, pledging to prevent future attacks and asserting the government's commitment to stability. Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop sought to reassure partners of the government's capacity to manage the crisis.

Economic Sovereignty & Reform: Despite the turmoil, the government pressed forward with major long-term initiatives. President Goïta inaugurated the Bougouni Lithium Mine, Mali’s second operational lithium mine, a project intended to boost economic sovereignty and generate over $380 million in revenue for the state. Additionally, the Council of Ministers approved key treasury reforms to enhance financial oversight and adopted new regulations for architects in line with UEMOA standards. The country also secured a $40 million loan from the IFC to expand agricultural lending and launched the Mali Drought Monitoring System (MaliDMS) to protect the crucial agricultural sector.

The transition government's stance on dissent continues to generate controversy. Former Prime Minister Moussa Mara was sentenced to one year in prison for expressing solidarity with political prisoners on social media, a ruling widely condemned by human rights groups. Furthermore, a prominent critic of the junta, Cheick Oumar Diallo, was reportedly forcibly disappeared by gendarmes. These events highlight tightening restrictions on free expression.

On a positive note, the government reached a landmark agreement to settle a 30-year-old dispute by allocating over nine billion CFA francs in compensation to former civil servants who accepted voluntary retirement between 1986 and 1993, an act described as "moral and social redress".

In summary, the military-led transitional government is facing the most serious test of its authority since seizing power, with analysts warning of potential political collapse or the rise of an Islamist republic. While the government is asserting its regional role-most notably by hosting the WCO-WCA Regional Customs Intelligence Meeting -and pushing forward a resource-driven economic agenda, its capacity to manage the escalating security and humanitarian fallout from the JNIM blockade in the coming weeks will be decisive for Mali's future stability.

title_en: Mali-UK Dialogue on Security and Stability
excerpt_en: On November 10, Mr. Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali, held a telephone discussion with the Right Honourable Baroness Chapman, Minister of State for Development and…
body_en:
On November 10, Mr. Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali, held a telephone discussion with the Right Honourable Baroness Chapman, Minister of State for Development and African Affairs of the United Kingdom.

During the call, Mr. Diop outlined the situation in Bamako and across Mali, highlighting hydrocarbon supply disruptions. He detailed the government's ongoing efforts to secure the territory and ensure regular supply, while denouncing a hostile media campaign against Mali. He reaffirmed the authorities' commitment to security, territorial integrity, and protection of people and property.

Baroness Chapman expressed the United Kingdom's solidarity with Mali and praised the government’s measures to restore normalcy. Both sides emphasized the value of a direct, frank, and constructive dialogue. Minister Diop reiterated Mali’s commitment to mutual-respect-based dialogue, while commending the UK for seeking information directly from national authorities.

excerpt: On November 12, Mr. Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali, received a high-level delegation of business leaders from Belarus on a working visit.
title_en: Mali Welcomes Belarusian Business Delegation
excerpt_en: On November 12, Mr. Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali, received a high-level delegation of business leaders from Belarus on a working visit.
body_en:
On November 12, Mr. Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali, received a high-level delegation of business leaders from Belarus on a working visit.

Minister Diop welcomed the economic exploratory mission, conducted amid a challenging security context and hostile media campaigns aimed at destabilizing the country. He presented Mali's new vision for integrated development, emphasizing economic transformation through diversified partnerships based on shared interests. The minister also highlighted the business climate, national economic landscape, and investment opportunities in strategic sectors such as mining, agriculture, transportation, industry, energy, and infrastructure.

Impressed by Mali's economic potential, the Belarusian delegation expressed interest in placing Mali on its economic agenda and developing a mutually beneficial partnership, reinforcing political and diplomatic relations. Both sides welcomed the convergence of views and stressed the need to continue sectoral exchanges to accelerate pragmatic economic and trade cooperation.

body_en:
BAMAKO, Mali-On November 12, 2025, on the sidelines of the Bamako International Defense and Security Exhibition (BAMEX 25), His Excellency Mr. Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, and Mr. Alhamdou Ag Ilyène, Minister of Communication, Digital Economy, and Administrative Modernization, held a press conference attended by numerous national and international media outlets.

Organized under the auspices of the Director of BAMEX 25, the conference was part of the government's communication strategy to provide the press with reliable information, countering a hostile media campaign aimed at destabilizing Mali.

The ministers stressed that hosting this international exhibition in Bamako, with participation from ten African countries and other regions, sent a strong signal amid the current geopolitical context. The event also refuted misleading information circulating abroad about Mali and its capital.

Joint efforts of the Malian defense and security forces and the AES Confederation to secure the territory and ensure the supply of hydrocarbons.

Implementation of a strategic plan to address ongoing challenges.

Condemnation of destabilizing actions fueled by media campaigns targeting Mali’s sovereign choices.

Main directions of the economic development vision.

The resilience of the Malian people, the courage of the armed forces, and the critical role of transporters.

Mali’s openness to balanced partnerships, based on new principles of public governance.

In conclusion, the ministers affirmed that nothing will hinder Mali’s sovereign progress, driven by the determination of the highest authorities, the support of the Malian people, and partnerships within the ESA Confederation and with friendly nations.

title: Mali Advances Women-Focused Peacebuilding Initiatives
excerpt: On Thursday, November 13, 2025, Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, and Lieutenant General Ismaël Wague, Minister of Reconciliation, Peace and National Cohesion and Acting UN…
title_en: Mali Advances Women-Focused Peacebuilding Initiatives
excerpt_en: On Thursday, November 13, 2025, Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, and Lieutenant General Ismaël Wague, Minister of Reconciliation, Peace and National Cohesion and Acting UN…
body_en:
On Thursday, November 13, 2025, Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, and Lieutenant General Ismaël Wague, Minister of Reconciliation, Peace and National Cohesion and Acting UN Resident Coordinator in Mali, co-chaired the National Steering Committee for the Peacebuilding Investment Mechanism in Mali. The session included the Chargé d'Affaires of Canada, UN Women representatives, and members of civil society.

The meeting focused on validating projects to be funded by the Women, Peace and Humanitarian Action Fund, ensuring compliance with eligibility criteria and alignment with national priorities.

The Steering Committee approved ten projects aimed at strengthening women's capacities in conflict prevention and crisis and emergency response, contributing to peacebuilding. The total budget for these initiatives is approximately US$1,158,000 (around 650,000,000 CFA francs).

Highlighting the significant progress made, the Committee emphasized the need for inclusive stakeholder involvement, adherence to national procedures, and regular operational monitoring and evaluation. Members urged all stakeholders to ensure the projects deliver meaningful impact for the population, particularly women, enhancing living conditions and fostering social cohesion.

title: Mali Reaffirms Sovereignty, Security, and International Partnerships at BAMEx
excerpt: BAMAKO, Mali-On the sidelines of the Bamako International Defense and Security Exhibition (BAMEx 25) (November 11-14), Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, accompanied by Alhamdou…
title_en: Mali Reaffirms Sovereignty, Security, and International Partnerships at BAMEx
excerpt_en: BAMAKO, Mali-On the sidelines of the Bamako International Defense and Security Exhibition (BAMEx 25) (November 11-14), Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, accompanied by Alhamdou…
body_en:
BAMAKO, Mali-On the sidelines of the Bamako International Defense and Security Exhibition (BAMEx 25) (November 11-14), Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, accompanied by Alhamdou Ag Iliane, Minister of Communication, Digital Economy, and Administrative Modernization, held a press conference with national and international media to reaffirm Mali’s security priorities, sovereignty, and development vision.

Minister Ag Iliane stressed that Mali, like any other country, is confronting an exceptional situation with determination and selflessness, while Mr. Diop reaffirmed that defense and security remain the absolute priorities of the Malian people.

He emphasized that Mali is at war against terrorism and separatism, facing three major threats described as the "trilogy of misfortune," involving Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM), Daesh (Islamic State), and an ongoing secessionist rebellion.

The transitional authorities are making considerable efforts, choosing to strengthen defense and security with sincere partners. The Malian Defense and Security Forces (FDS) have achieved resounding successes on the ground, defeating terrorist groups and their leaders. Thanks to the FDS's firepower, these groups have been forced to change strategy, now targeting more vulnerable locations.

Regarding external pronouncements predicting the fall of Bamako, Minister Diop categorically refuted these claims as "fabricated" by foreign intelligence services and amplified by television studios. He affirmed that Mali remains strong, is neither Syria nor Afghanistan, and possesses sufficient military capabilities to deter any threat, describing the hostilities as a "proxy war" by hybrid forces.

The government has implemented a strategic plan to secure convoys and restore the country’s supply, particularly to Bamako, with hundreds of trucks arriving daily. The challenge lies in transport security, not product availability, with FDS personnel, transporters, and private operators risking their lives to ensure deliveries. Mali does not require specific external assistance to manage this situation.

body_fr:
BAMAKO, Mali-On the sidelines of the Bamako International Defense and Security Exhibition (BAMEx 25) (November 11-14), Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, accompanied by Alhamdou Ag Iliane, Minister of Communication, Digital Economy, and Administrative Modernization, held a press conference with national and international media to reaffirm Mali’s security priorities, sovereignty, and development vision.

Minister Ag Iliane stressed that Mali, like any other country, is confronting an exceptional situation with determination and selflessness, while Mr. Diop reaffirmed that defense and security remain the absolute priorities of the Malian people.

He emphasized that Mali is at war against terrorism and separatism, facing three major threats described as the "trilogy of misfortune," involving Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM), Daesh (Islamic State), and an ongoing secessionist rebellion.

The transitional authorities are making considerable efforts, choosing to strengthen defense and security with sincere partners. The Malian Defense and Security Forces (FDS) have achieved resounding successes on the ground, defeating terrorist groups and their leaders. Thanks to the FDS's firepower, these groups have been forced to change strategy, now targeting more vulnerable locations.

Regarding external pronouncements predicting the fall of Bamako, Minister Diop categorically refuted these claims as "fabricated" by foreign intelligence services and amplified by television studios. He affirmed that Mali remains strong, is neither Syria nor Afghanistan, and possesses sufficient military capabilities to deter any threat, describing the hostilities as a "proxy war" by hybrid forces.

The government has implemented a strategic plan to secure convoys and restore the country’s supply, particularly to Bamako, with hundreds of trucks arriving daily. The challenge lies in transport security, not product availability, with FDS personnel, transporters, and private operators risking their lives to ensure deliveries. Mali does not require specific external assistance to manage this situation.

Mali is working closely with the Confederation of Sahel States (CSA), including Burkina Faso and Niger, to break the cycle of dependence, subjugation, and external domination. Partnerships with countries such as Russia and Turkey, represented at BAMEx, signal support based on respect, trust, and solidarity.

The ministers also emphasized Mali's openness to balanced partnerships, the resilience of the Malian people, and the courage of the armed forces, underscoring a vision for autonomous action, strategic autonomy in defense, and the integrated development of the country.

title: The rise of terrorism in West Africa dominated debates at the United Nations Security Council in
excerpt: The rise of terrorism in West Africa dominated debates at the United Nations Security Council in New York, where UN Secretary-General António Guterres and the President of the ECOWAS Commission, Omar Alieu Touray…
title_en: The rise of terrorism in West Africa dominated debates at the United Nations Security Council in
excerpt_en: The rise of terrorism in West Africa dominated debates at the United Nations Security Council in New York, where UN Secretary-General António Guterres and the President of the ECOWAS Commission, Omar Alieu Touray…
body_en:
The rise of terrorism in West Africa dominated debates at the United Nations Security Council in New York, where UN Secretary-General António Guterres and the President of the ECOWAS Commission, Omar Alieu Touray, jointly sounded the alarm.

Their shared message: the threat is no longer confined to the Sahel or the Lake Chad Basin. It has spread across the entire West African region, posing an existential risk to millions of people.

Guterres emphasized that terrorism, once geographically localized, now strikes across a much wider arc, affecting both rural areas and strategic routes. In recent months, armed groups have repeatedly attacked escorted military convoys, killing and abducting soldiers and civilians. These actions are intended not only to spread terror but also to deliberately disrupt access to fuel, goods, and essential services, creating what he described as an “economic war”.

The consequences are severe: fuel shortages have forced some humanitarian operations, including those run by the UN, to scale back activities, threatening vulnerable populations. Guterres warned that the combination of insecurity, shortages, and the collapse of services could trigger a “catastrophic domino effect” on coastal countries such as Benin and Togo.

In response, ECOWAS Defense and Finance Ministers have considered establishing a regional intervention force, with an initial deployment of 1,650 troops and plans to scale rapidly to 5,000 soldiers. Guterres stressed that close cooperation between states is essential to strengthen the region’s security and political architecture.

Omar Alieu Touray reinforced this warning with sobering figures: between January and November 2025, the region experienced 450 terrorist attacks, resulting in over 1,900 deaths. He described terrorism as an existential threat to West Africa, highlighting the fragmentation of regional efforts, mistrust between states, and insufficient international funding.

Touray explained that extremist groups aim to isolate populations by blocking fuel access, disrupting trade, and cutting supply routes, thereby weakening communities and complicating security responses. He called for sustainable solutions that address root causes, including poverty, lack of public services, weak governance, and marginalization.

Both officials concluded that the region urgently needs consistent international support, particularly predictable humanitarian funding. Needs for 2025 amount to $4.9 billion, yet only one-quarter is currently covered. They urged strengthened cooperation, better coordination among regional forces, and renewed political commitment to prevent the crisis from spreading further across the continent.

title: Algeria Urges Inclusive Political Solution as Mali Faces Escalating Terror ThreatsAlgeria, November 18, 2025
excerpt: Algerian Minister of State and Foreign Affairs, Ahmed Attaf, has issued a stark warning regarding the deteriorating situation in Mali, emphasizing that the current surge in terrorist threats carries unpredictable…
title_en: Algeria Urges Inclusive Political Solution as Mali Faces Escalating Terror ThreatsAlgeria, November 18, 2025
excerpt_en: Algerian Minister of State and Foreign Affairs, Ahmed Attaf, has issued a stark warning regarding the deteriorating situation in Mali, emphasizing that the current surge in terrorist threats carries unpredictable…
body_en:
Algerian Minister of State and Foreign Affairs, Ahmed Attaf, has issued a stark warning regarding the deteriorating situation in Mali, emphasizing that the current surge in terrorist threats carries unpredictable consequences for the entire Sahel-Saharan region. Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Minister Attaf recalled that Algeria had anticipated these developments nearly two years ago, when “the Malian authorities unilaterally denounced the Agreement for Peace and Reconciliation stemming from the Algiers process.”

Attaf stressed that Algeria’s approach to security and stability is comprehensive and cooperative, rather than isolated or self-serving. “The current situation in Mali, with a resurgence of terrorist threats reaching unprecedented levels, concerns and worries us more than anyone else,” he said, citing both geographical proximity and Algeria’s historical commitment to supporting Mali through crises since its independence.

He reaffirmed Algeria’s long-standing support for Mali’s territorial integrity, unity, and sovereignty, stating:"Algeria has always been, and remains, one of the most fervent defenders and supporters of preserving the unity of the Malian state, its territory, its people, and its institutions. We affirm Mali’s full, complete, and uncompromising sovereignty."

Recalling a statement from January 26, 2024, Attaf warned that “the military option constitutes the first and greatest threat to the unity of Mali and the integrity of its territory, as it carries within it the seeds of civil war, while undermining national reconciliation efforts and posing a real threat to regional security and stability.” He noted that current events in Mali confirm these earlier predictions.

The Algerian minister underscored that the Malian crisis cannot be resolved through military means or exclusionary approaches. He called for:

Responsible dialogue and comprehensive reconciliation among all Malian citizens, without discrimination or foreign interference;

Recognition that national unity is the only path to confront terrorism effectively and address broader regional security challenges.

Concluding his remarks, Attaf reiterated Algeria’s commitment to its neighbor: “We remain open to our brothers in Mali, exercising inexhaustible patience to address the current crises in our neighborhood with wisdom, serenity, and discernment.”

title: JNIM Escalates Blockade; Multiple Countries Urge Citizens to Evacuate Mali
excerpt: Mali, November 18-19, 2025 - Following JNIM’s announcement on November 18, 2025, of the launch of the second phase of its fuel and supply blockade, several European nations issued urgent travel advisories.
title_en: JNIM Escalates Blockade; Multiple Countries Urge Citizens to Evacuate Mali
excerpt_en: Mali, November 18-19, 2025 - Following JNIM’s announcement on November 18, 2025, of the launch of the second phase of its fuel and supply blockade, several European nations issued urgent travel advisories.
body_en:
Mali, November 18-19, 2025 - Following JNIM’s announcement on November 18, 2025, of the launch of the second phase of its fuel and supply blockade, several European nations issued urgent travel advisories. Norway, Denmark, and Sweden formally called on their citizens to evacuate Mali immediately on November 19.

These warnings came on the heels of alerts from fifteen other countries, including the United States, France, and Portugal, which had previously cautioned their nationals about the heightened risk of kidnappings and attacks targeting foreigners amid the deteriorating security situation.

Authorities emphasized that the resurgence of JNIM activity, combined with ongoing fuel shortages and attacks on convoys, presents serious threats to both residents and expatriates, underscoring the need for vigilance and rapid response to the evolving crisis.

excerpt_en: Washington, November 19, 2025 - The Algerian Ambassador to the United States issued a strong statement on November 19, underlining Algeria’s perspective on the escalating crisis in northern Mali.

Washington, November 19, 2025 - The Algerian Ambassador to the United States issued a strong statement on November 19, underlining Algeria’s perspective on the escalating crisis in northern Mali. He described the region as a “natural extension of Algeria,” highlighting the shared ethnic groups, communities, and historical ties that link the two countries.

The ambassador emphasized that Algeria’s security remains a top priority and firmly rejected any form of foreign interference along its borders, signaling the country’s intent to closely monitor and manage developments in neighboring Mali.

This statement follows recent warnings by Algerian authorities regarding the resurgence of terrorism in Mali and reflects Algeria’s ongoing commitment to the stability and territorial integrity of the Sahel-Saharan region.

title: Russia Assists Mali in Combating Fuel Shortages Amid Jihadist Attacks
excerpt: Mali, November 20, 2025 - In a press briefing on November 20, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Maria Zakharova detailed the involvement of the Russian Army Corps for Africa in Mali’s ongoing fuel crisis.
title_en: Russia Assists Mali in Combating Fuel Shortages Amid Jihadist Attacks
excerpt_en: Mali, November 20, 2025 - In a press briefing on November 20, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Maria Zakharova detailed the involvement of the Russian Army Corps for Africa in Mali’s ongoing fuel crisis.
body_en:
Mali, November 20, 2025 - In a press briefing on November 20, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Maria Zakharova detailed the involvement of the Russian Army Corps for Africa in Mali’s ongoing fuel crisis. According to Zakharova, the crisis began in mid-September, triggered by systematic attacks on fuel convoys by the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (GSIM), an Al-Qaeda affiliate, targeting shipments primarily from Senegal and the Ivory Coast to Bamako and other regions.

Zakharova described the spread of disinformation by jihadist groups, exaggerating the severity of the fuel blockade and the Malian authorities’ inability to respond, with the explicit goal of sowing discontent and pressuring the transitional government.

At the request of the Malian authorities, the Russian Army Corps for Africa has been actively deployed on the ground, providing checkpoint security, convoy escorts, air support, and search operations. Zakharova reported that jihadist fighters are incurring heavy losses and that recent days have seen a reduction in the severity of the fuel shortage.

Russia reaffirmed its commitment to supporting the Malian people, aiming to help them overcome current challenges and move toward sustainable, self-reliant development.

title: U.S. Warns of Al-Qaeda Expansion in Mali and the Sahel
excerpt: United Nations, November 18, 2025
title_en: U.S. Warns of Al-Qaeda Expansion in Mali and the Sahel
excerpt_en: United Nations, November 18, 2025
body_en:
United Nations, November 18, 2025

Mike Waltz, United States Ambassador to the United Nations, issued a stark warning regarding the deteriorating security situation in Mali and the wider Sahel region. Speaking at the UN on November 18, Waltz described the situation as catastrophic, noting that Al-Qaeda-affiliated terrorists have effectively paralyzed Mali by targeting and blocking fuel supplies, exacerbating the humanitarian and security crisis.

Waltz emphasized that the threat is not confined to Mali alone, but is spreading southward. He cited recent terrorist attacks in Benin and Togo as evidence of the expansion of extremist influence in West Africa. According to the Ambassador, these developments indicate that Al-Qaeda is actively seeking to seize control of the entire country, with implications for regional stability and international security efforts.

The statement underscores the urgency for coordinated international and regional responses to prevent further territorial and humanitarian collapse in Mali and the Sahel.

title: Algeria Reaffirms Strategic Interest in Northern Mali
excerpt: Washington, D.C., November 19, 2025
title_en: Algeria Reaffirms Strategic Interest in Northern Mali
excerpt_en: Washington, D.C., November 19, 2025
body_en:
Washington, D.C., November 19, 2025

Sabri Boukadoum, Algerian Ambassador to the United States, underscored the deep historical, ethnic, and cultural ties between northern Mali and Algeria, describing the region as “a natural extension of Algeria: same ethnic groups, same people, same vision.” Speaking on November 19, Boukadoum emphasized that Algerian security is a national priority and firmly rejected any foreign interference at its borders, while advocating for inclusive dialogue to address the ongoing crisis in Mali.

The ambassador also characterized Mali as a “failed state,” highlighting the stark north-south divide: the northern regions suffer from a lack of resources and essential services, presenting a significant development deficit compared to southern Mali. Boukadoum stressed that these structural weaknesses make the north particularly vulnerable to terrorist exploitation, further threatening regional stability.

This statement reflects Algeria’s ongoing commitment to regional security and mediation in Mali, reaffirming its role as a key actor in addressing the Sahel-Saharan security and governance challenges.

title: AU Special Representative Meets Malian Foreign Minister to Strengthen CooperationBamako, Mali - November 17, 2025
excerpt: Dr. Mamadou Tangara, the newly appointed Special Representative of the Chairperson of the African Union Commission and Head of the AU Mission for Mali and the Sahel (MISAHEL), was received on Monday, November 17, 2025…
title_en: AU Special Representative Meets Malian Foreign Minister to Strengthen CooperationBamako, Mali - November 17, 2025
excerpt_en: Dr. Mamadou Tangara, the newly appointed Special Representative of the Chairperson of the African Union Commission and Head of the AU Mission for Mali and the Sahel (MISAHEL), was received on Monday, November 17, 2025…
body_en:
Dr. Mamadou Tangara, the newly appointed Special Representative of the Chairperson of the African Union Commission and Head of the AU Mission for Mali and the Sahel (MISAHEL), was received on Monday, November 17, 2025, by His Excellency Abdoulaye Diop, Mali’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, as part of the presentation of his credentials.

During the meeting, Minister Diop and Dr. Tangara reviewed key areas of cooperation between Mali and the African Union, considering both national partnerships and the broader confederal dimension in light of evolving sub-regional geopolitical realities.

Minister Diop welcomed the AU’s constructive approach to dialogue and reaffirmed Mali’s commitment to Pan-Africanism. He highlighted the need for partners to take into account Mali’s current situation and stressed the importance of fostering a sincere, frank, and constructive dialogue to strengthen African solidarity amid global challenges affecting the region.

Dr. Tangara, in turn, assured that the African Union would actively contribute to solutions in Mali, expressing his commitment to strengthening the partnership and addressing ongoing challenges while respecting Mali’s principles and interests. He emphasized his personal attachment to the country and his dedication to supporting its stability and development.

title: Confederation of Sahel States (AES) Calls for Sovereign-Led Regional Cooperation Against Terrorism
excerpt: New York, United Nations Security Council - November 18, 2025
title_en: Confederation of Sahel States (AES) Calls for Sovereign-Led Regional Cooperation Against Terrorism
excerpt_en: New York, United Nations Security Council - November 18, 2025
body_en:
New York, United Nations Security Council - November 18, 2025

At a public briefing on “Peacebuilding in West Africa: Revitalizing Regional Cooperation in the Fight Against Terrorism in West Africa and the Sahel”, a representative of the Confederation of Sahel States (AES) delivered a statement on behalf of the foreign ministers of Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, who were unable to attend due to scheduling conflicts.

The representative commended the leadership of Sierra Leone President Julius Maada Bio, chairing the Security Council, for convening the debate on revitalizing regional cooperation to combat terrorism in West Africa and the Sahel. Scope of the ThreatThe AES emphasized the escalating terrorist threat in the Sahel, highlighting that for over a decade, communities across the region have been subjected to violence imposed and supported by external actors. Women, children, and civilians have been killed, kidnapped, or forced into exile, while schools and health centers have come under attack. In response to the increasing inability of local Defense and Security Forces (FDS) to contain these threats, criminal networks have turned to economic terrorism, targeting civilian infrastructure and supply routes.

excerpt: As part of ongoing political exchanges with the United Nations, His Excellency Mr. Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali, held a working meeting with a UN delegation led by Mr.
title_en: Mali Strengthens Cooperation with UN Amid Rising Regional Security ChallengesBamako / New York - November 20, 2025
excerpt_en: As part of ongoing political exchanges with the United Nations, His Excellency Mr. Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali, held a working meeting with a UN delegation led by Mr.
body_en:
As part of ongoing political exchanges with the United Nations, His Excellency Mr. Abdoulaye Diop, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali, held a working meeting with a UN delegation led by Mr. Leonardo Santos Simao, Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for West Africa and the Sahel, in the presence of the Acting UN Resident Coordinator in Mali.

The meeting is part of Mali’s efforts to strengthen cooperation, support, and solidarity with the UN in addressing current regional and global security challenges. Minister Diop provided a comprehensive assessment of the situation in Mali, detailing the government’s actions to respond urgently and effectively across multiple fronts. Particular emphasis was placed on the fight against state-directed terrorism, which leverages political, geopolitical, military, economic, and media instruments.

Diop highlighted the transformation of Mali’s armed forces from units once heavily dependent on international aid to a force now exhibiting operational autonomy, capable of safeguarding the territory of the AES Confederation-the sole theater of operations for its Defense Forces-and preserving broader sub-regional stability.

The Minister also denounced the interlinked threats of economic terrorism and media-driven disinformation, particularly those propagated by certain foreign media outlets, noting their role in disrupting supply chains and amplifying social unrest. He praised the efforts of the Transitional Authorities in ensuring essential services and supporting a population demonstrating resilience and awareness of the crisis’s broader implications.

Discussions extended to issues of peace and reconciliation, particularly the National Charter for Peace and Reconciliation, which remains Mali’s primary framework for conflict resolution. Sub-regional cooperation was also addressed, including integration of the AES Confederation’s security and development dimensions into dialogue with the UN. The meeting underscored the role of UN agencies, funds, and programs in improving living conditions for Mali’s population and reinforcing collaborative mechanisms to stabilize the Sahel.

Minister Diop concluded by reaffirming Mali’s commitment to constructive engagement with the UN, promoting regional solidarity, trust-building, and sustainable solutions to ongoing security and socio-economic challenges.

title_en: Amid persistent deterioration of the security situation, France is reducing its diplomatic staff in
excerpt_en: Amid persistent deterioration of the security situation, France is reducing its diplomatic staff in Mali, following similar measures by the United States and the United Kingdom, which have already repatriated their…
body_en:
Amid persistent deterioration of the security situation, France is reducing its diplomatic staff in Mali, following similar measures by the United States and the United Kingdom, which have already repatriated their non-essential personnel. French authorities strongly recommend temporary departure for French nationals and discourage all travel to the country.

Mali continues to face frequent attacks from JNIM (affiliated with AQIM) and the Islamic State, further exacerbating insecurity in both rural areas and along key strategic routes. These conditions have made diplomatic and humanitarian operations increasingly difficult.

The ongoing fuel blockade has triggered significant economic hardship, with multiple cities experiencing prolonged shortages that disrupt daily life and fuel social tensions. This economic strain, combined with direct threats against civilians and business operators, has intensified the climate of insecurity.

JNIM has threatened to classify truck drivers as combatants and urged NGOs, businesses, and associations to oppose the Malian transitional authorities. While some fuel deliveries have reached Bamako, the situation remains critical, with the potential to worsen rapidly if no immediate solutions are implemented.

Economy and Tech.

excerpt: In a bid to address growing trade disruptions caused by rising insecurity in Mali, the Malian Minister of Transport and Infrastructure, accompanied by the Director General of the Senegalese Port, visited the Autonomous…
title_en: Mali and Senegal Collaborate to Unblock Critical Dakar-Bamako Trade CorridorDakar/Bamako - November 21, 2025
excerpt_en: In a bid to address growing trade disruptions caused by rising insecurity in Mali, the Malian Minister of Transport and Infrastructure, accompanied by the Director General of the Senegalese Port, visited the Autonomous…
body_en:
In a bid to address growing trade disruptions caused by rising insecurity in Mali, the Malian Minister of Transport and Infrastructure, accompanied by the Director General of the Senegalese Port, visited the Autonomous Port of Dakar on November 21, 2025. The meeting focused on resolving bottlenecks along the Dakar-Bamako trade corridor, where over 2,000 containers, including high-profile shipments such as the Marian container, remain stranded, directly affecting Mali’s supply chains and commercial flows.

The Malian Minister noted that some containers remain within their permitted free time, while others have exceeded it, highlighting the urgency of coordinated action to mitigate economic losses.

The visit aimed to develop an evacuation plan in collaboration with Senegalese carriers to ensure the safe and efficient movement of goods along the corridor, overcoming obstacles posed by jihadist activity and heightened insecurity in transit regions.

The Director General of the Port of Dakar, Walid Boudon, reaffirmed Senegal’s commitment to supporting Mali and underscored the importance of regional cooperation in maintaining trade continuity despite security challenges.
